utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, to continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of your knowledge - that's where we broke off yesterday - America did take part in Operation Storm in which over 200.000 Serbs were expelled. Lord Owen called it the greatest ethnic cleansing in all the conflicts in Yugoslavia, and the mass killing of vast numbers of civilians. A permanent member of the Security Council took part in ethnic cleansing that started from UN protected areas and they were placed under the protection by that same Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is already a question that is turning into a statement. The first part of the question, "To the best of your knowledge America did take part in Operation Storm where 200.000 Serbs were expelled" is a collapse of the alleged involvement by America, if any, in Operation Storm with what is said to be the overall results, and it's clearly a tendentious question in the form of a statement, and the accused should confine his question to something that this witness can really answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. It's not sufficiently relevant. I'm not allowing it. Move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why Mr. Nice is so nervous about all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on to another question. I've already ruled on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Colonel Barriot, yesterday we broke off when you explained that, in contravention of any kind of authority given to them by the United Nations, the Americans took part in Operation Storm. Tell us, what do you know about that operation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My answer will be a very clear one. This is not an alleged participation by the United States as was underlined just now by Mr. Nice. It is a proved fact, it is a proved participation on two levels. On the one hand you have a direct military intervention and participation because in the very first days of the Storm operation the US air force had two jets coming from the Roosevelt warship that bombed Knin. So this was a direct participation of the US army in the very beginning of the Operation Storm, with application of securing the airspace in the Krajina so that there could be an intervention by the Croat army. And on the other hand you have an indirect intervention through this private military company, MPRI Incorporated, which is a military private company depending on the Pentagon. And these specialists intervened as instructors and also as advisors of the Croat army in order to carry out the Operation Storm. But we also saw instructors from that company during the Storm operation in the territory of the Krajina, especially in Knin. And this was stated unambiguously by Canadian soldiers who were in Knin at the time. Therefore, the US participation is not an alleged one. It has been a direct intervention -- both indirect and direct intervention, and it has been proved as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in Krajina, at the time of the conflict between the Muslim forces in the Bihac pocket, according to the information I have, is it correct that there were 40.000 Muslim refugees in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can confirm the figures. This happened during the summer of 1994. The 5th Corps of the BH army in the Bihac pocket was headed by General Atif Dudakovic and it launched an attack especially in the area of Velika Kladusa, and it expelled up to 40.000 Muslims who were faithful to Fikret Abdic. These 40.000 Muslims were expelled towards the Krajina area, and they were taken in two camps which I personally visited together with people, officials from the UNHCR. Bertrand Dupasquier was a responsible official at the time. These 40.000 people were taken in the Batnoga and Turan camps where they were taken care of with a lot of humanity by the local population in Krajina. The local population fed them but also looked after them medically speaking; if they were wounded, if they were sick, if they were women about to deliver, they were taken care of. So all these Muslims were gathered in Batnoga and Turan and they were taken care of in the Glina Hospital with total dedication. They were given blood supplies. They were helped without any kind of discrimination. And very often the few medicines, the few supplies that there were in the Glina Hospital were given to the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These refugees, these 40.000 Muslims who came to Krajina, could they have gone to Croatia or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was impossible for them to get out and to seek shelter in Krajina or elsewhere. The only opening for them or the only possibility offered to them later on was a return to the Bihac pocket early in 1995. And it is precisely in the Bihac pocket that the large amount of them were massacred during the Operation Storm by the 5th Corps of the BH army, but also by Croat troops that had infiltrated in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was a double standard involved in terms of treating the Muslim population itself; those who were on Alija Izetbegovic's side received support whereas those who were on Fikret Abdic's side were exposed to all kinds of persecution, destruction and the like?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Muslims who were on the side of Fikret Abdic, including these 40.000 expelled refugees, were practically victims of persecution by the Muslim and Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite. Absolutely. In 1994, it was obvious that the central authority in Sarajevo and that Izetbegovic's army was trying everything possible to eliminate both Fikret Abdic and to remove all the Muslims in the Bihac pocket faithful to the latter. So they were exposed, and they were victims of the central authority in Sarajevo, and they also fell prey to the Croat forces which were intent on removing any kind of support to the Krajina Serbs, support by the Muslims who were in the Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the authorities of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina? Was it clear to them that since these Muslims had no where to go that a considerable number of these people could stay on in Krajina forever?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my view there was no problem whatsoever regarding taking in the Muslims in the Krajina Republic, because even before the 5th Corps was created in the Bihac pocket, it was obvious and it was frequent that Muslims would come from Velika Kladusa, from that area towards Glina where they were taken care of, they were looked after, and they could remain very safely in that area and also in Banija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Barriot, I would like to hear your comment concerning a quotation that I'm going to read out to you from this so-called Croatian indictment. It is count number 6. I have a revised copy only in the English language, so count 6 says: "[In English] The purpose of this joint criminal enterprise," [Interpretation] and previously it says: [Previous translation continues] ... "[In English] joint criminal enterprise. The purpose of this joint criminal enterprise was the forcible removal of the majority of Croat and other non-Serb population from the approximately one-third of territory of the Republic of Croatia. That he planned to become part of new Serb-dominated state through the commission of crime," et cetera. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond [Interpretation] Can you comment upon this? What kind of enterprise could this have been if they were taking in such a large number of Muslims or, rather, non-Serbs, taking care of them, not expelling them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the question itself reveals its inappropriateness. It is not for the witness to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he can comment on fact situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He can -- he can give evidence of facts, but he cannot give comments, and the comments that he's invited to give is a comment that is for the Judges to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you must reformulate the question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, the fact that you spoke of, that is to say the acceptance of so many thousands of Muslims in the area of the Serb Krajina, does that preclude any possibility of these authorities having some kind of plan of expelling the non-Serb population from that area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see how he can answer that. He can't answer that question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Maybe he will be able to answer another question later on that also has to do with these manipulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, before that, let us go back -- or, rather, can I just ask you to be as brief as possible in your comments regarding a document which is under tab 27 of the exhibits that will be introduced through you, and that is an official document of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 20th of December --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: September, interpreter's correction, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No translation, I think, has yet been provided. I'll check.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. You have been given a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be within the Crepin ones. I haven't done a cross-reference. Tab 26 of Crepin I think is the same document, so we do have it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tab 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have 27 as well in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 27 in Barriot is, I think, tab 26 in Crepin, and we have been provided with an English translation at tab 26 in Crepin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we have it in English, yes. Go ahead, Mr. Milosevic. You must point us to the particular section in tab 26 to which you are referring.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the last paragraph. Just the last paragraph. It is in the context of what we've been discussing. It has to do with an investigation based on the 11th of September, and it says the document was signed by the director and the two deputy directors of the service, and it was sent to the president of the Council of Ministers of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that paragraph says: "The same day (at 1932 hours), Interpol Wiesbaden sent us a request for a check on a person called Atta who, according to their information, is said to have lived in a small village called Bakotic, 8 kilometres from Maglaj in 1999." So it's 1999. "They enclosed a copy of a photograph of Mohammed Atta who was supposed to be identified by a man called Mehmet Hasanic from the village of Bakotic. We forwarded the Interpol Wiesbaden request to the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and so on and so forth. This is a person who piloted one of the planes that hit the World Trade Centre, Mohammed Atta. I assume that everybody knows about that. And I showed the review conducted by Izetbegovic of an entire brigade of Mujahedin near Maglaj. And this man was in Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1999, and this indicates that he was there earlier on as well, which shows that this terrorist network was well rooted in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us your comment about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. Don't ask him to give a comment. You must ask a specific question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, all right, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this yet another confirmation of the existence of this terrorist network in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? In this case, it is directly linked to the events of 9/11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is nothing to suggest that, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was a completely leading question in substance and form. I can't keep standing to object to them, but I'm sure the accused, who is now an experienced operator in this courtroom, knows the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, yesterday you, in response to me, explained how evidence of terrorism in Bosnia could be relevant to specific charges. I'd like you to rehearse that, because I'm still troubled by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In many respects this particular line of questioning was not something I had anticipated or known about. As the Court knows, I don't have instructions on it. I think the position we have here is as the accused put in the question about it being -- terrorism being well rooted in the region, and it is attempt by the Defence here to link the established and well-rooted links with terrorism to events that were taking place during the parameters of the indictment. That's been a fairly consistent approach, or a very consistent approach by the accused during the trial, and this is an example of -- a very well-known example of the man Mohammed Atta who was held responsible, amongst others, for the 11th of September hijacking and terrorist incidents in the US, to show that from information received he was able to be identified as having been within Bosnia-Herzegovina at a particular time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kay. You had -- had you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Milosevic, we'll allow the questioning along these lines, but it has to be fairly specific and focused. I mean, ultimately we have to be satisfied about relevance to particular charges in the indictment, how the question of terrorism affects the question of guilt or innocence arising from the charges in the indictment. And on the basis that there is some relevance in terms of the defence that you're raising, we'll allow it, but we intend to monitor this line of questioning very closely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Colonel, before Mr. Milosevic asks you another question, can I ask you how you came by this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was provided by intelligence services, and I was authorised to present them because they were not classified as secret by the French government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, does this document corroborate the fact that terrorism was well rooted in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. But before I answer this question, I'd like to underline the paradox there is to be found in Mr. Nice's argument. He was challenging the credibility of my testimony yesterday because I failed to provide concrete information or failed to show specific links with intelligence services whilst today I'm introducing evidence of the fact that this terrorism is well rooted and he'd like to challenge that as well. He would like me not to present these documents and me not to comment on them. So my answer will be this, and it will be a very clear answer. This comes from the Ministry -- Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you answer, I should make it clear I certainly don't understand Mr. Nice's position to be as you've indicated. Mr. Nice has taken no objection to the production of the document. The objection is to some of the questions that are posed, which are entirely inappropriate. So you must understand that you're not being unfairly treated by the Prosecutor here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, before the witness answers -- Mr. Milosevic, I'm returning to this linkage of terrorism with the charges in the indictment. If you can establish that terrorism was well rooted there, where does that take us in terms of your Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my introductory presentation, I explained that the Western countries supported in Croatia the forces of Nazism in Bosnia, in Kosovo, the forces of Islamic fundamentalism and terrorism is what I said, and that is completely contrary to any healthy reasoning. And everything was used and utilised for the frameworks of this criminal enterprise launched against the Serbs. You saw how things developed in Croatia, how they developed in Bosnia, how paramilitary formations were formed in Bosnia, who took part in them. And if all those are positive phenomena, then there's no need for me to go and explain them. But with respect to the instructions and guidelines you gave a moment ago, Mr. Robinson, I have understood it so far that it is my right or, rather, the right of somebody accusing somebody of something has the burden of proof and that the burden of proof is not on the accused to prove his innocence, whereas you keep explaining the former -- or, rather, the latter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I'm going to stop you. Let -- let -- I have stopped you, Mr. Milosevic, because the comment shows that you don't understand the function of the Chamber. We have a duty to admit evidence but only evidence that is relevant, and that applies as much to the Defence as it does to the Prosecution. And I'm having some difficulty, perhaps I'm speaking for myself, in understanding the linkage between well-rooted establishment of terrorism in Croatia at the time and -- in Bosnia and the question of your guilt or innocence. I see it in a tangential way, but I'm still not fully satisfied. Perhaps it is my own weakness. I can see some marginal relevance and it is on that basis that I'd allow the question, but the questioning has to be very specific and focused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask your question now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, does this represent confirmation of the assertion about the well-rootedness of terrorism in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've stayed out of this debate as much as I can, but I must suggest, with all due deference, that an appropriate approach to the questioning by the accused of this or any other witness on this topic could or should be limited as follows: If the existence of terrorism on the territory is relevant or may be relevant, then it would be open to the witness to simply produce a document such as this to show the existence of the man Atta on the territory at a particular time. I note parenthetically that the man Atta was present on a number of other European territories over the broad period of time as well. I hope it doesn't have a similar significance for those countries. His evidence, however, should be limited to the fact of the presence of a terrorist on the territory. He should not be allowed to be asked questions of the kind that have just been asked, which are leading in substance and form and have no value and are indeed really covering the territory that has to be covered in due course by -- The only other way in which questions might be of value is this: If the accused is able to ask of a witness, "Do you know of a terrorist or did a terrorist show involvement in or commit one of the crimes with which I'm charged," fine, obviously relevant, but it's as far as that and no further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what about specific questions about terrorist acts committed in Bosnia against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can see that potentially of significance if it may change the overall picture, yes, but it is, of course, a specific question. Yes, I wouldn't object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there is merit in the points taken by Mr. Nice. You could ask him if he was aware of the presence of -- of terrorists or of a specific person, but -- I mean, but to ask -- I'm not allowing you to ask him to confirm that the paragraph establishes or goes to show that terrorism was well-rooted. The document is before us, and we can read it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since Mr. Nice raised the question of whether these were used against the Serbs, then I shall continue on from that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, did the terrorists in Bosnia, were they used against the Muslims in -- with the aim of placing the burden on the Serbs and responsibility in accusing the Serbs of the crimes which they in fact had committed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So it will be a question in different forms. I will give very clear names of Islamic terrorists. I give you the names of Kelda Hubet [phoen], who was in Bosnia, and Christophe Caset, Lionel Dumont, Urad Puguran [phoen]. So I have quoted specific names of people who were connected to the Islamic network, so with connections with the GIA and al Qaeda that operated in Bosnia against the Serbian forces and Serb civilians, and also operated against French people in France. I mentioned today the presence of Mohammed Atta in a Bosnian village in 1994 and 1995. He was also present there in 1999. We also have pictures showing the presence of Mirsad Asahawi [phoen], formerly Izetbegovic in the 1990s. So these are very clear facts clearly indicating that these people were not just travelling around and dropping off in a hotel in Sarajevo over 48 hours. These were terrorists that had gone to terrorist training camps in Bosnia, Kosovo, and the north of Albania. So I think things are very clear on that point. These were terrorists actions. And to answer the question put by President Milosevic, we have knowledge and understanding of a number of terrorist acts conducted by Bosnian Muslims at the time. More specifically, attacks against French Blue Helmets. Let me also mention that there were -- there were 56 French Blue Helmets who died between 1991 and 1995, and two-thirds of the French Blue Helmets were targeted by the Muslim snipers on the orders of Mr. Izetbegovic. I think nobody can deny this. Now, as far as these terrorist attacks against Sarajevo are concerned, I would like to mention that all French ballistics experts on the 27th of May, 1992, attack, or the Markale attack on the 5th of February, 1994, as well as the attack against Markale on the 2nd of August, 1994 are not due to Serb fighters but to Muslim snipers. You can question what I'm saying, of course, but you can also then question Lewis MacKenzie, the Canadian general; Sir Michael Rose, the British officer; Jacques Longsade, who is the Chief of Staff of the French army. Also you then question Pierre-Marie Gallois, the founding father of nuclear deterrence in France, and a number of personalities in the French government, and I can quote you further details if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Colonel Barriot, the question you were actually asked there is whether terrorists were used to attack Muslims with a view to placing the blame on Serbs. Now, did you actually answer any -- was any part of your answer directed to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The second part has to do with the explosions in Sarajevo which were conducted by Muslim terrorists against the Muslim population in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What -- what information or evidence do you have in answer to Mr. Milosevic's question that this was done with a view to Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond placing the blame on Serbs? Are you in a position to address that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, well, the Serbs were accused of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. You must allow the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So there are a whole series of evidence and statements which have been provided in the wake of these facts. I -- I have described them to you rather briefly. If you so wish, I have all the statements of the French officials and French generals regarding these facts and stating clearly that one could not accuse the Serbs of these explosions, but these explosions had been conducted by -- at the hands of the Muslims. I can read out these statements if you so wish. May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think you have answered the question. Perhaps you are not in a position to. Mr. Milosevic, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a brief digression, if I may, one question. You were in Topusko, Colonel Barriot; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet someone called Slobodan Lazarevic there; and if so, what can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet Mr. Slobodan Lazarevic on several occasions because he was taken part in the briefing sessions of UNPROFOR in Glina. He was a rather strange person which nobody took very seriously and who spoke about a lot of things and then denied them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you that question because he was one of the witnesses presented here by the other side over there. So that's why I wanted to draw your attention to that. Now, Colonel Barriot, as far as Bosnia is concerned, you were in contact with Radovan Karadzic, weren't you? I assume that you talked to him about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And what was the contents of those talks you had with him?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met President Radovan Karadzic on several occasions, and more specifically in 1995. As I mentioned yesterday, I also published an article in my book, The Murder of a People, Serbs of Krajina, and I also brought along a French television crew that conducted reports on President Karadzic, some of which were broadcast and others were not. During these interviews with President Karadzic, we primarily talked about the political situation, the overall political situation in Bosnia, and we talked about the way fundamentalism was running out of control, and this was a matter of great concern to President Karadzic. We discussed in great detail the situation in the Bihac pocket, because he felt that this was quite indicative of the tension mounting between the fundamentalism movement of the SDA of Izetbegovic and the moderate Muslims, on the other hand, that wanted peace with the Serbs. What comes to mind more specifically here is Fikret Abdic. He stressed the fact that Fikret Abdic was the man who should be entitled. According to the elections in 1990, Fikret Abdic was the natural leader. He mentioned assassination attempts carried out by Izetbegovic's men to do away with Fikret Abdic - he was threatened on several occasions - and military operations of the 5th Corps of the BH army, which was again supported by the US army, because all the Muslim fighters of the 5th Corps were equipped with assault rifles, M-16s, which came from the US army, and this was in total contradiction with the arms embargo at the time. Ever since the elections, little by little fundamentalist government had done away with its Serb and Croat partners but had also done away with moderate Muslims in Bosnia who, I repeat, had remained loyal to Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to draw your attention to the fact that the interpretation into the Serbian language, if we can call it Serbian at all, is very poor. I assume that we're not talking about lack of knowledge but quite simply things are not being interpreted if they don't -- if the interpreter doesn't feel that they need to. I noticed that yesterday. This is what it says in English: "Ever since the elections, little by little fundamentalist governments had done away with its Serb and Croat partners but had also done away with modern Muslims in Bosnia [In English] remained loyal to Fikret Abdic." [Interpretation] We're talking, in Serbian, I hear "integrism" mentioned, and quite simply, the interpretation into the Serbian language is being distorted, so please bear that in mind because I'm not going to tolerate that any more. That happened yesterday and there is no sense in having that continue. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a terrible assertion to make about the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's a terrible assertion to make about the interpreters. And if the accused is able to identify some particular either shortcoming or difference in interpretation from that which he would have preferred, then he can always raise it, and he should raise it in a neutral way and the interpreters could then be given a chance, when matters are fresh in their memory, to deal with what he is asserting. But it is quite inappropriate for him to make the sort of assertion he has made about people who serve this court faithfully for several years and work in extremely hard circumstances, not least circumstances made difficult by the rapidity of questions and answers that they have to deal with. So that on this particular occasion he has said that there was a reference to "integrism," as he has used the word, which hasn't been reflected. I would invite the Chamber to allow the interpreters to explain whether they heard the word, and if so, how they interpreted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Your comments are very appropriate. Mr. Milosevic, your comments were ungracious and completely neglect the hard work that the interpreters have done. They have worked proficiently. I'm going to ask you to identify the particular passage which you say was misinterpreted and then ask the interpreters to comment on it. I believe it was a reference you said to integrism in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're talking about Islamic fundamentalism here, and that of course is understandable for anybody following these proceedings. I don't think more than half the people here could understand what the integrism --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or "integralism," interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that is something we can't understand. I'm looking at the transcript and I'm listening to the interpretation. So I don't see why I can't raise an objection to something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course you can. You must do so in a manner that is appropriate and that reflects due consideration for the hard work which interpreters have to do here. And I must say, speaking for the Chamber, we find that their work is of the highest standard. This doesn't mean that a mistake cannot be made now and then. So that for "integrism" you're saying that the reference should be to "fundamentalism"; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what it says in the transcript. I don't know what should have been said, but that's what the transcript recorded, "Islamic fundamentalism" as it was translated and recorded by the transcript. So I'm listening to the interpretation and looking at the transcript. But let's not waste time. I made the objection and I hope that they will pay attention to the interpretation. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would like to say that the Chamber does not approve of the manner in which you made the objection. Mr. Nice is perfectly correct. These proceedings must be conducted with a decorum that is appropriate to the nature of the work, the gravity of the work that we are doing here, and you must show due respect to the interpreters, and we will not tolerate that kind of comment. If a mistake is made, then you must bring it to our attention and we will see to it that it is corrected if it is to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask the interpreter to comment on this particular passage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. It's the interpreter of the Serbian booth. I am practically certain that -- I mean, I am certain that I heard the word "integrisme" in French. The English booth translated it as "fundamentalism" and I translated it in Serbian as "integrism," which I consider to be closer. Mr. Milosevic was not referring to the original, which was in French and which was "integrism" but to the translation into English, which is just one of the two translations, and ours was into Serbian and I consider it was faithful. But you can, of course, check it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we have the explanation, and we will move on. And, Mr. Milosevic, bear in mind what I've said about the attitude, your attitude towards the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a negative attitude to the interpreters, but I expect them to conduct themselves properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, I, speaking for myself, consider that you owe the interpreter in this instance an apology unless you dispute what she's just said to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not only that mistake that I'm objecting to. I cannot follow everything, of course. There are completely incomprehensible parts of sentences, whether somebody is opposed to someone or opposed to who. You can't get the gist of it, who is opposed to what. And if we take a look at the tape, then I'll be able to compare. I can't go into comparative linguistics now, whatever. I was just doing the comparison between what I was hearing from the Serbian, in the Serbian, and what was recorded in the transcript. So there are more mistakes. I wouldn't have reacted if it were just that one mistake. So I don't see why I would have to apologise to the interpreters, Mr. Bonomy, and I of course cannot listen to the French in the original. It was not I who made the mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you accepting what the interpreter has said about this matter or are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the word "integrism," yes, the explanation, but not as regards the context of the whole translation, the interpretation, which is, when it comes to the Serbian interpretation, is quite incomprehensible at times. But whether she's going to say "integrism," whether the interpreter is going to say "integrism" in one way or another isn't that essential. I just hitched on that point and took -- brought up that difference. But let's move on because my time is moving on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, I won't allow you to make a general criticism of the interpretation in the manner in which you have just done. You say that it is quite incomprehensible at times. If you find that a mistake has been made, a mistake, in your view, has been made, then you must bring it our attention, but it is absolutely unfair and unacceptable to make a general criticism of the interpretation without pointing to specific misinterpretations. That's not -- that's not playing fair at all and is totally unacceptable. And I'd like to say on behalf of the Chamber that we find that the interpretation generally has been of a very high standard and we express our gratitude to the interpreters for the work that they have done and continue to do. Proceed with the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, we left off discussing your conversation with Karadzic. Did you discuss anything else except the Bihac pocket, the conflict with the Muslims, for example, and so on and so forth? Do you wish to stress some important point or can we just move on?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to stress two points. After these conversations I had with President Karadzic, he repeated often times that the 20th century had seen the emergence of an unnatural alliance of the Croatians and Serbs, and he hoped that the 20th century would see an alliance between the Croatians and the Serbs to fight Muslim fundamentalism in Bosnia. That is the first thing I remember clearly after these discussions we had. Secondly, at this time we talked about the breakaway from Belgrade, and I remember quite clearly when he said that this breakaway is not due to us but this is no solace either. He also said often times that he never received any orders from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand this now. In the Serbian language, I heard "secession." The word "secession" was used, whereas in the English it's "the breakaway from Belgrade," according to the transcript. So I don't know what "the breakaway from Belgrade" means, or the rift from Belgrade. And I really can't say what the witness said in French.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I repeat what I said. In the course of these discussions where a number of French journalists were present, we discussed the rift or the distance between the Serbs in Bosnia and the authorities in Belgrade. And what I was saying is that President Karadzic was saying that in effect there had been a rift between the two and he was saying that it wasn't due to him, but he was saying also that that was no consolation either. He also stated that he did not receive any orders from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You met General Mladic several times; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met him, Karadzic, several times -- Mladic, sorry, in 1995, and more specifically in June 1995 in Bijeljina, in September 1995 in Banja Luka. And it's at that time also that I published an article by him in my book and that I authorised French television crews to conduct interviews of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to put two questions to you now that have to do with talks with General Mladic and then you're going to tell me whether you discussed that or not, but I'm interested in the following: Did you speak more precisely about what was going on in the UN protected areas, what happened in Sarajevo? Was there any mention of what was going on in the eastern enclaves, in the Bihac pocket? Did you discuss these important issues, if I can put it that way, or did you discuss some of them, at least?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. I spoke with General Mladic on the one hand about the general military situation prevailing in Bosnia, and then we talked about the security zones, especially about Sarajevo, and then about the eastern enclaves. Of course, we also spoke about Srebrenica. So I'll say yes, we mentioned all the issues you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is of course perfectly open to you to call General Mladic as a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you intend to arrest him on the basis of his being a witness here, then I certainly do not want to call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just saying it's a matter for you, but you could call him as a witness in your Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a minute ago that you talked about Srebrenica. You said a few minutes ago that you saw him in September 1995 in Banja Luka; is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then, what was it that you found out about what happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall be very clear as to the unfolding of these events. I can state that I have this information directly from General Mladic. On the one hand, I can stress once again, because General Mladic would insist on this very often, that Srebrenica should have been a demilitarised zone as early as 1993, but it wasn't at all. It sheltered an entire division of the BH army. The troops under Naser Oric spread terror around Srebrenica in the Serb villages for several years, from 1992 to 1995. Naser Oric's militia killed 1.500 to 2.000 people in the area. Everybody remembers the Kravica village massacre during the Orthodox Christmas in 1993. General Mladic would often speak about the massacre by Naser Oric's militia in the area in order to account for the resentment and the fear of the Serbs towards the militia, his militia. And General Mladic mentioned often that these forces were found in a zone protected by the UN which should have been demilitarised. As to the Srebrenica events, General Mladic would insist on the events that took place just before the Srebrenica battle. He would insist on the fact that whilst the UN, the UNHCR had recommended to Mr. Izetbegovic that the women and the children should be evacuated and sent somewhere safe because there might be an attack by the Serbs, but Sarajevo very decidedly refused to do so, refused to evacuate women and children until July 1995. General Mladic also insisted on the fact that it was the Sarajevo government that had ordered Naser Oric to withdraw and to withdraw his staff from the town of Srebrenica before the attack. So there was an obvious decision and deliberate intention not to defend the town and not to ensure the safety of its inhabitants. He insisted a lot on that. Now, regarding the events that took place in July 1995, this is how the events unfolded as was related by General Mladic: During the attack or the battle that occurred on the 11th of July, 1995, there were some 40.000 inhabitants in Srebrenica. Twenty-five thousand of them were mainly women, children, old people, and they surrendered to the forces of General Mladic. These 25.000 civilians were never in danger. They were transported towards Kladanj and towards Tuzla in Muslim territory, and nothing, nothing was -- no harm was done to them. Out of these 25.000 people, there were about 750 men that were held prisoners because their identity was to be checked and it had to be checked that none of them was suspected of crimes against Serbs in the area. Out of these people, 500 were not suspected at all. They were released, and they were able to go towards Kladanj and Tuzla. Two hundred and fifty of them were held back because there was suspicion against them. They were suspected of crimes against the Serbs. They were detained in Zvornik and Batkovic, and it is probable that out of these people there were some summary executions because some Serbs recognised some of the authors of some crimes in their villages, but according to General Mladic, no more than hundred summary executions took place out of this group of people. Regarding the actual battle that took place in the night of the 11th to the 12th of July, 1995, in the surrounding woods, some 15.000 Muslims, armed Muslims, came out of Srebrenica in that night of the 11th to the 12th. This figure was confirmed by Naser Oric himself. And out of these 10 to 15.000 men, they were confronted in the woods in the night with General Mladic's army, who expected a ferocious battle against well-armed Muslims. So of course there were fights during the night. The Serbs, conducted by General Mladic, lost over 500 men, and the armed Muslims lost some 1.500 to 1.800 men. So this is what actually happened in Srebrenica on the 11th and the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This narrative is just too long, and it's not an acceptable way of receiving evidence. You must ask -- ask another question and get a specific answer to the question. To have the witness speak for five, ten minutes is just -- it's not -- I don't even remember the question that he's answering. And we have discussed this before. I want questions asked, and I want short answers where that is possible. Of course some answers will be longer than others.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's just the way you put it, Mr. Robinson; "whenever possible." I think that my question was quite appropriate, the one I addressed to Colonel Barriot: "What was it that you found out from General Mladic about Srebrenica?" He is a person who talked to General Mladic in September 1995, and he briefly related what he learned from him about the events in Srebrenica and that's all. And I don't see anything inappropriate in that. There are no facts on the basis of which I could put brief questions to him that would only entail yes or no answers. I simply asked him what he found out from General Mladic and that's what he related to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not yes or no answers. Not necessarily yes or no answers, but an answer which takes five to ten minutes doesn't help because it's difficult to digest. It's difficult to understand. So you are in charge of your examination-in-chief. After he has spoken for a short time, two or three or four sentences, you must intervene, come in again with another question. That's the way I would like the evidence to be given. I'm not in support of what is called the narrative approach to evidence where witnesses speak forever. It does not conduce to an understanding of the evidence. So please ask another question and let us have an answer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Barriot, what you said, would that be the gist of the explanations that General Mladic gave to you in relation to what happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm sorry, Mr. President, regarding something as serious as Srebrenica, regarding the talks that were long, it would be absolutely abnormal to be reduced to three minutes of explanation to relate discussions that took place over several hours and something as tragic and as important as the battle in Srebrenica. I insist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is not for you to insist. That's totally out of order. You will answer the question in the way that I have directed or not at all. Do I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. I insist on the need to answer the questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is not for you to insist on anything. It's not for you to insist on anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You will answer the question in the way that it was asked and along the lines that I have suggested. I don't want a narrative of five to ten minutes which is difficult for anybody to understand. Mr. Milosevic, you are leading the witness. You come from a system in which this is not the practice. Examination-in-chief and cross-examination are not part of the civil law system. In this part of the case we are following an adversarial system. If you follow Mr. Nice when he's examining in chief, he does not allow a witness to speak for five, ten minutes. That's the way I want it to be done and that's the way it will be done while I'm presiding here. I will not allow answers that roam far and wide and last for five, ten minutes, because that's not helpful. So if you want him to relate what his understanding of what happened in Srebrenica, do it in bits and pieces. I will not allow a narrative of five, ten minutes from the witness. You have assumed responsibility for examining in chief, and you must do it in accordance with the procedures that the Chamber approves. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond If you want more from him on Srebrenica, he can give more, but I don't want him to speak for five, ten, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to make one comment on this, though. I've -- or I understand that question quite differently, I think, from the witness. Mr. Milosevic seemed to me to be making the point that all the witness had done was give the gist of the account that Mladic gave him, that obviously the account would be much lengthier, but the gist was all that was necessary for the purposes of the trial, and the witness, instead of simply saying yes to the question embarked on a long -- or sought to embark on a further narrative that was quite unnecessary. So the fault at the moment seems to me to lie with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put a specific question and let us have a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long did your conversation with Mladic last then in September 1995, as you said, when you met with him?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spent several hours speaking together in the Banja Luka barracks, and President Milan Martic was there, along with other people, but there was also a French television crew which took part in part of the discussion, not in all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the French television crew take part in that portion of the conversation when you talked about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The French television crew were there mainly to interview General Mladic regarding the fact that the French pilots had been taken prisoners and to talk about the terms for their release, but they also mentioned Srebrenica. But the French crew were not there at all the meetings and discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, during that conversation that you had, did General Mladic give any other explanations as to how come a number of prisoners of war were killed in Srebrenica? Did you talk about that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He mentioned the possibility indeed of some executions, there again because there was so much hate accumulated between the Serbs and the Muslims in the area that it was inevitable for some executions to take place, because the Serbs of the area recognised some Muslim militia of Naser Oric who had massacred their families. So obviously it cannot be doubted that there were some settlements of accounts, but never was any order given for a massacre or the execution of prisoners by him. That is obvious. That cannot be doubted at all. And he also insisted chiefly on the fact that Srebrenica was a strategic objective. He attacked Srebrenica in order to neutralise Naser Oric's militia, not at all in order to eliminate the population of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, when you say that "never was there any order given for a massacre or the execution of prisoners by him. That is obvious. That cannot be doubted at all," is this what was related to you by General Mladic or is that your own assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was stated. He was quite sort of adamant about it. There was no single execution of a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're relating what he said to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. That's precisely what I wished to ask the witness, is this exactly what General Mladic said to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was General Mladic who said to you that there were absolutely no orders to execute prisoners. That's what he said to you in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can confirm that again. I can support what I said totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. There is no need to go through it again. All right. Now we are briefly going to deal with your stay in Kosovo. In June 1998, you were in Pristina. Please tell us in the briefest possible terms what the situation was like when you came to Pristina then. Can you describe the situation to us?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I shall be very brief. I arrived in Pristina in July 1998, or June 1998. The situation was then very tense because it was practically impossible to just walk about in the streets of Pristina together with Serbs, because the Serbs felt that they were threatened. I met at length Rector Radivoj Papovic. I had long conversations and discussions with him, and I then told him I wished to go to the southern area in Kosovo. I wanted to go to Pec and Decani in particular. Rector Papovic said I should not do that, I should not go through Kosovo because the roads were blocked by the KLA on the one hand but also because two Croat generals of Albanian origin, Ademi, Ceku notably, were in the area and they had all reasons to have resentments towards the Serbs in the -- towards the representatives of the Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Colonel Barriot, when did you go to the south of the province? After that, you did go to Pec after all, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I did. In July and August already I went towards the southern area in Kosovo, and I had in my pocket a letter by Patriarch Pavle. He had asked me to support and aid the Pec hospital because there was a lot of fighting in the area. The hospital was overwhelmed, and Patriarch Pavle thought it was useful to send me to Pec so that I could help the hospital doctors look after the wounded. So I went to Pec in July and August 1995 -- 1998, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to read a brief quotation to you now from this so-called Kosovo indictment, and then I'm going to put a question to you. That's count 87 for you gentlemen. It says here: "[In English] In late 1990 and 1991, thousands of Kosovo Albanian -- of Kosovo Albanian doctors," [Interpretation] and so on, "[In English] dismissed from their positions." [Interpretation] Now it says that Albanians -- or, actually, you were in the hospital and doctors were referred to. You were dismissed from your own job. Tell me, what kind of medical staff did you find employed at the Pec hospital when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of such a statement. It's hard to believe it. Indeed a large part of the medical staff and paramedical staff in the Pec hospital were of Albanian origin, so I couldn't tell you exactly what the ratio was but one thing was certain; there are more Albanian doctors and nurses than Serb doctors and nurses, and that was the case in the Pec hospital where I worked for several weeks in 1998. And there were so few Serb doctors that in the summer of 1998, medical teams had to come from Serbia or from Kragujevac in Kosovo in order to help me and to bring additional assistance, because there were very few Serb doctors and nurses at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just in the interest of accuracy, paragraph 87 reads: "Throughout late 1990 and 1991, thousands of Kosovo Albanian doctors, teachers, professors, workers, police, and civil servants were dismissed from their positions." I think you stopped at "doctors."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did because I did not consider this witness to be competent to give answers in relation to the others. I quoted this so that I could compare it to the situation that he found at the Pec hospital as far as the medical staff is concerned, to compare it with this position contained here. Because it is asserted here that in 1990 and 1991 Albanians were dismissed from their jobs, and he was there in 1998, and now he says that the majority of the medical staff, the majority of the doctors, the majority of the nurses, of all staff, were Albanians. So this is just one of the falsehoods contained here, and there's really no point even commenting on it. This could not happen in a single civilised country, to put these kind of things on paper, but paper will suffer anything, won't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot -- Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are now at the time for the break. And in future you must avoid comments of that kind. We will break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Barriot, a moment ago you were talking about the facts which had to do with the structure of the hospital staff. Just tell us briefly, what about the patient make-up? What was the structure of the patient composition?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: So as I was in the Pec hospital in the summer of 1998, there were essentially two kinds of injured people. There were on the one hand a great number of Serbs that were coming in every day, whether they were civilians or members of the police forces that had been injured and had been wounded by bullets. And there was a second category of wounded people. These people were Albanians, generally speaking moderate Albanians that had been beaten up by members of the KLA because of their friendly attitude vis-a-vis the Serbs, either because they had had a drink with them or because they had showed signs of friendship towards the Serbs. So these people were -- had generally been beaten up. They had broken limbs, broken jaws due to -- because they had been hit with some sharp objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you yourself are a humanitarian worker and officer and were there for a significant period of time, if I can say so, tell us, please, what was the situation like with respect to the rights of the Kosovo Albanians, for instance?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can testify to the fact that I -- I was in the -- working for the patriarch of Pec. I was working on a daily basis in the Pec hospital, and I moved around on foot in the town, and I went to the market every day. I also went or drove around the whole region by car. We went to Decani and that entire area. So what I can say is that I have at -- I have never witnessed any violent attitudes on the part of Serbs or the Serb forces vis-a-vis the Albanians. And the presence of Serb forces in Pec at the time was minimal and was not something which was particularly striking at the time. What I can also say is that the Albanians, the Kosovo Albanians, were never discriminated, as far as I could see. And they spoke Albanian. And when I went to the market or I went to march and I said "avijenje" [phoen], "good-bye" they picked me up in a rather aggressive way and said to me that I should say goodbye in Albanian, in the Albanian language. We saw the flourish of a number of the Albanian flags, the black eagle against a red background. We saw this on a number of houses. Also in the streets you could see people handing out posters and leaflets calling for the independence of Albania. So I think it is quite clear that the situation in the summer of 1998 in this particular region, I can say there was no discrimination or no violence carried out at the hands of the Albanian population on the part of the Serbs or carried out by the Serb forces. There were a number of newspapers around. It was very easy to find newspapers in the Albanian language. It's much easier to find Albanian newspapers than it was to find Serbian newspapers. There were hardly any Serbian newspapers, as a matter of fact, to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the activities of the KLA during that period of time, and how would you characterise those activities if you do have knowledge of them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that the UCK had mistreated a number of people, and these mistreatments were of different kinds. There was, on the one hand, people had been attacked, there had been ambushes laid against the Serb police forces, and this resulted in a number of deaths. There had been a number of Serb people had been abducted, particularly in the centre of Kosovo, in the central region of Kosovo. Some villages had been completely burnt down and the Serb people had been expelled from these villages. So we saw a surge of violence at this time, and this was conducted by the KLA militia. I would call these terrorist attacks since -- insofar as these people targeted civilians primarily, whether they be Serb civilians or the refugees from the Serb camps in Krajina. I visited a number of centres where the refugees had been placed, and they were savagely attacked by the KLA militiamen. This violence was not only targeted at Serb civilians but also at moderate Albanian civilians when the latter had not been involved or were not part of the separatist movement of the KLA. Pec is close to the border -- is on the border with Albania. Pec, Levubinje [phoen]. There is a lot of drug trafficking on these borders and the Serb forces were trying to counteract this arms and drug trafficking which was crossing the border at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that all you know about the activities of the Serb forces and security forces at that time or do you know something more? What were the activities, to the best of your knowledge? What kind of activities were in force by the Serb forces and security forces of Serbia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I do know as regards the activity of the Serb forces at the time is that these Serb forces were responding or retaliating to the attacks and the ambushes. So this was very clearly targeted and in line with the violence against them. It was aimed at protecting the civilian population. As I said, not only the Serb civilians but the non-Albanian minorities like the Romas and the moderate Albanians in Kosovo. The Serb forces therefore were protecting the civilians and were retaliating to the KLA attacks on a case-by-case basis and were trying to counteract these groups being infiltrated on the border with Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any personal contact with a compatriot of yours and your colleague, Bernard Kouchner, for instance, and do you know anything about his involvement in the events in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Bernard Kouchner is a colleague of mine. I met him personally in 1991 because he sent me to Kurdistan, the Iraqi part of the country, and I had a close contact, personal contact with him. Now, as regards his approach to the Yugoslav conflict, I believe that he clearly demonstrated that he took sides, because the two associations he created would be Medecins du Monde and Medecins Sans Frontieres which are two associations which sided quite clearly and did not respect the neutrality which such organisations should respond to. In other words, these organisations which were created by Kouchner, which were to protect the Muslims in Bosnia and also sided with Kosovo in Albania and totally disregarded the suffering of the Serb people during this war. I also believe that Bernard Kouchner, who was administrator of Kosovo, I think went well beyond the scope of the 1240 UN Resolution which granted him his mandate. He ordered the expulsion of the last Serbs still remaining in Kosovo. I think Bernard Kouchner probably left the same souvenir as Kurt Waldheim in the mountains of Kozara left. So he went beyond his mandate, and as we saw what happened in March of 2004, the UN mission fell short of its requirement and could not prevent the expulsions of the last Serbs remaining in Kosovo. I also question the honesty of Mr. Kouchner. I think it's -- he is an unnatural result or combination between the political situation and the army. I'm sorry. I just wanted to say that it is because of Mr. Kouchner that we don't know today whether the hospitals are there to protect patients or armed militia. We don't know whether ambulances are transporting patients or arms. And during this war, in 1993 in particular, we discovered large stashes of weapons under the Medecins Sans Frontieres humanitarian aid packages which were designed for the Muslim enclaves, the same way we discovered in Kosovo in the ambulance rocket Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond launchers belonging to or destined to the KLA. I think this is something which Mr. Kouchner was largely instrumental in and led to the lack of neutrality of the NGOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm more than a little concerned about the nature of this extended answer. Let me make it straight away clear: Of course I have no interest here to serve in defending anyone who happens to be named, but it is one thing for the witness to give evidence of facts, he appears to be able to do, of discovering items in particular vehicles or places, but it's another entirely for him to be allowed to say the sort of things that he's saying at page 39, line 21, and to make assertions about the honesty of a public servant. I repeat, I have no role to defend the person but there must surely come a time when unless it is absolutely and clearly relevant, this sort of comment should not be tolerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We hear the submission, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Colonel Barriot, do you have any knowledge about the support that the terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija received?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These KLA terrorists in the Kosovo-Metohija region were supported by a number of factions. On the one hand they were, of course, supported diplomatically by Madeleine Albright, Richard Holbrooke in the region. Let me remind you that when Richard Holbrooke, in the autumn of 1998, went to Kosovo, Osama bin Laden was actually in the Northern Albania at the time. They were supported, likewise, by William Walker and all American diplomats. They were also supported by Croatian generals of Albanian origin, General Rahim Ademi and Agim Ceku were present in the region. Agim Ceku was charged with coordinating the movements of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, with such extraordinary wide-ranging allegations, none of which is our function to defend necessarily or to deal with, might it be at least helpful if the witness identified the piece of paper or the precise source of his knowledge for some of these assertions that he's making. Because otherwise, and we know what's going to happen, the assertions will be picked up because they are attractive fodder for certain types of media outlets, particularly in the former Yugoslavia, and they will be given a prominence they simply don't deserve, which may be unfair on those named and may of course not reflect properly the way this case is being conducted. I made an observation in a recent filing that there may be reason to be concerned about the accused using his opportunity to ask questions and to elicit evidence turning into a propaganda exercise of a kind that's irrelevant to the trial but potentially harmful in the future, and I would invite the Court to be cautious about allowing the sort of rein that this witness is taking in making the sort of broad assertions he's just made, linking all sorts of names without identifying his source material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a matter that you could take up in cross-examination, and the position that I've taken or the doubt that I've expressed about the relevance of terrorism doesn't apply to this part of the case. It relates to the Bosnia part of the case. I don't see the relevance. But here the KLA is definitely relevant, and if he has evidence of support for the KLA, I would think that that is relevant evidence. It is, of course, open to you to refute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not necessarily challenging that, and of course there's the opportunity in cross-examination, but when one sees the artful, it may be, linking of high-profile names together in consecutive sentences and drawing broad conclusions, I would invite the Chamber to be cautious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your concern, but I think there is a basis here for the -- for that kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I'd like to emphasise to the witness to make his evidence more specific. Let me give you an example. You said in an earlier answer, "On the one hand they were --" yes, this is it. You said, "Let me remind you that when Richard Holbrooke, in the autumn of 1998, went to Kosovo, Osama bin Laden was actually in Northern Albania at the time. They were supported, likewise, by Mr. William Walker and all American diplomats." It is an overly general statement without any specific comments. It's nothing to the Chamber. So Mr. Nice is referring to this overall generality in his submission. Then Mr. Milosevic should pursue more specificity from the witness. Bearing this in mind, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Barriot, on what basis did you observe that Holbrooke and the rest of the people you mentioned lent support to the KLA or, rather, the terrorist groups in Kosovo and Metohija, and what do you know -- but, never mind. That will be my next question. Answer this one first, please. What was the basis for you to make your observations?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the one hand, when I talked about Srebrenica earlier on and I gave details, I was told I was too slow, and when I try to be more concise and just talk about what is essential, I'm told I'm too detailed. So I shall go into this in detail. As far as General Agim Ceku is concerned, he was a general who was in charge, or one of the senior people in charge of the Operation Storm against the Serbs in Krajina. At the time he was responsible or running MPRI, and I -- he was in charge of the armed branch of the KLA in 1999. He was appointed chief of the operations in Kosovo, and he was appointed by the Americans. I think these are very clear facts which took place at the time. As far as William Walker is concerned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, the interpreters are asking you to slow down. I know you're eager to give the evidence, but speak more slowly so that the interpreters can follow. And bear in mind that the question you are answering, what is the basis for you to make your observations, it's the question of support. What is the evidential basis for saying that these high-ranking Americans were supporting the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the information I got from French and foreign intelligence services at the time I was there. So I believe that I retrieved firsthand information as regards this particular case. I should also like to emphasise that transmission equipment was provided by the KLA, by the French intelligence and German intelligence services. So diplomatic, military and material support was given by the Western intelligence services, and this was given to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the crimes of Ceku in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If I may and if I still may -- still may quote some names, Agim Ceku was a member of the Croatian forces who conducted the massacre in the Medak pocket in 1993 with Janko Bobetko, and together with Ceku there was also Ante Gotovina and General Mirko Norac, so these generals were responsible for the invasion and attack on Krajina and Operation Storm in August 1995, and they also were guilty of crimes against civilian populations in Krajina. And as far as Rahim Ademi, he went from Krajina to Kosovo and there is great reason to believe that he was involved in the Klecka massacre in the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's stay with Ceku for just a moment. His crimes in the Medak pocket, I assume, were something that was -- people knew about. How do you explain the fact that despite a clear knowledge about the great crimes committed by Agim Ceku, he himself was nominated commander of the Kosovo Protection Corps when the United Nations took over control of Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all this is very clear. This has to do with the connections with the Americans, with the United States, because during Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Operation Storm, he was one of the main people in charge. He was there, establishing contact with MPRI, and he held the same position in Kosovo, where he was in charge of coordinating the movements of the KLA together with Military Professional Resources Incorporated was also present in Kosovo and Macedonia. And I would like to stress this. Ante Gotovina also said that if ever he were to be captured, he would talk about everything he knew about the connections between the Croatian forces, MPRI, the US army and what happened in Krajina in August of 1995. I think Mr. Ceku knows enough about all of this and will probably never be called upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1994, Colonel Barriot, you wrote a letter to your paper Le Monde. What was the contents of that letter and what was the response you got?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we come to that, because I can't quite see how a letter to Le Monde is likely to be relevant and its answer less so, I should perhaps respectfully draw to your attention that the accused indicated he was going to take, I think, an hour and a half with this witness. He's already taken two hours and 40 minutes. We've made the point before and we don't resile from it that it is substantially a matter for the accused how he either uses or it may be wastes the time available to him, but if the Chamber is concerned about the relevance or marginal relevance of some of this evidence, it may be it would want to have in mind the fact that the time limit has already been getting on for doubled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
