utterances.text: Some of the time was taken up, Mr. Nice, in legal argumentation about the relevance of evidence, matters raised by the Chamber itself. So I'd like to take account of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But have we limited the time for examination in chief in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, we haven't limited it. It's just his own indication. He's set his own budget, and I just draw to your attention he's almost doubled his time. Almost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That will not be lost on Mr. Milosevic. He attends to these matters very carefully, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat that question. You wrote a letter to Le Monde. What did it contain, and what was the answer?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This letter is important because it clearly shows the state of mind at the time and how the media reacted at the time. In 1994, let me repeat, this was a time when there was fighting in the Bihac pocket between the governmental forces of Sarajevo, the 5th Corps of the Bosnian army, and the moderate Muslims of Fikret Abdic. I was worried about this and I sent a letter to Le Monde to underline the suffering and persecutions the moderate Muslims were suffering from, those that were loyal to Fikret Abdic. Let me just quote one sentence of this very well known French paper. "We cannot share your interpretation between Fikret Abdic and Irakovic [phoen] who was acting in the name of an essential government in the face of a threat of secession." The media always took sides or took the side of the government in Sarajevo in the same way as they took sides for the government in Zagreb against the people who were wanting to secede. But in Kosovo, when the Albanians found themselves in the identical situation, they were then supported. So it's a double-standard system which I think clearly is indicated in this letter. On the one hand you had to support Sarajevo against Fikret Abdic, Tudjman against the Serbs in Krajina, but on the other hand, when there was not, to support Belgrade against Albanian secessionist. I think double standards were applied all the time during this war and the three moments, important moments in this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Barriot, just a few short questions. You looked at the effects of different types of weapons professionally. To what extent was the -- were the weapons used by NATO created an effect on the civilians or had an effect on the civilians? How did it affect the civilians and the possibility of them staying in their own homes and houses or deciding to flee?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I shall be very brief. This is my speciality, and I can spend days talking about it. Different weapons were used by NATO, and these hit civilians. What comes to mind is the fragmentation bombs or cluster bombs which were used in the sites of Kosovo, and we know full well that these cluster bombs don't explode instantly, and when they don't, they operate like anti-personnel mines and had killed a number of children in the sites of Kosovo. Graphite bombs, which led to power cuts in hospitals which resulted in a number of deaths in hospitals, particularly in the reanimation centres and for newly-born children. Uranium 238, which led to the contamination of the ground and the whole of the food chain, which would probably lead to a number of cancer -- cases of cancer and malformation. What comes to mind also is the bombing of chemical industrial sites. When you destroy with a standard bomb a chemical industrial site, you contaminate the environment for a number of decades. So the Pancevo complex was destroyed, the Novi Sad refinement was destroyed, Kragujevac Zastava site was destroyed, Bor complex were destroyed also. There were thousands of tonnes of chemical products, sulphur dioxide, a number of extremely toxic products were released in great quantities, in tens of thousands of tonnes, which will lead to very adverse effects for the people living there. All these attacks were not aimed at the Serb forces because they were not hit, but these targeted primarily civilians and are, therefore, crimes against humanity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're a man of many parts, Colonel Barriot. Colonel, I was saying that you're a man of many parts. You're a doctor, you're an expert in arms, and now you're a lawyer. I see you have characterised this as a crime against humanity. That's a matter for the Chamber. So I'll thank you to avoid legal characterisations which are a matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, in view of the operations that you could assess professionally, what was their effect on the general feeling among the population, namely, in terms of deciding whether they would stay at home or whether they would flee their homes? I'm talking about Kosovo and Metohija where the bombing was intensive, 24 hours every day, round the clock. So the point is, how could this affect the citizens in terms of them deciding whether they're going to stay at home or whether they're going to flee? How did this affect civilians?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before answering your question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you answer that, could you provide us with the basis for your giving an answer of this kind? Were you present or is this answer going to be on the basis of information that you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to say that I was in Serbia in March and April of 1999, so I can say that I got -- I saw these bombs coming down. I was in Belgrade at the time of the bombing. I saw with my own eyes the destruction of the radio television building in Serbia. I saw the destruction of the Chinese embassy as well as a number of -- the Pancevo complex and a number other civilian buildings. I was there, on the one hand. I was also in contact with a number of Serbian -- Serb doctors, and I received their reports. Let me remind you that I've just written a book on arms systems. I would also like to say that when I -- what I said was not of a legal nature but of a medical nature. When I talk about crimes against humanity, I'm talking in medical terms and not in legal terms. So to answer President Milosevic's question, of course the civilian population was never warned and the children in Kosovo who would played in the fields cannot be warned that there are cluster bombs around. In the same way, the farmers in Kosovo who drink the milk and eat their Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond salads do not know and cannot detect 238 uranium in the ground. In the same way, when the NATO military conducted investigations, they were wearing very heavy protected suits, whereas people were never warned and never protected in any way and were never told about the risks that they were incurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Barriot, now I'm going to talk about the entirety of your experience that you gained over a rather long period of time in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. In terms of everything you saw in Krajina, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in Kosovo and Metohija, does that correspond to what you could find in the media of your country and other Western countries and in the statements, public statements made by statesmen in your countries?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. There is a total split, and I indeed think of the fact that I have, through the many years I experienced that, a good overview of the situation. What was hidden from the public opinions in those countries is the fact that in Croatia, in Bosnia, and in Kosovo the Serbs were not at all aggressors but, on the contrary, were in a state of legitimate self-defence in the face of an aggression. Vukovar did not start in November 1991 with the fall of the city. It started in August of that year, starting with the abuse by Mercep's militia. Srebrenica did not start either in 1995. It started in 1992, and it started with the aggression by Naser Oric's militia. So there is a distinction that was made between the first initial aggression and the response, whilst the Serbs only responded. I showed it for Bosnia and Kosovo. The Serbs tried to answer and to face a threat by terrorists, by fundamentalists often coming from abroad. So the hands of the Serbs were tied in their backs so they could not exert their right to self-defence. That's what I noted. And I insist on saying that many military and senior officers made the same observations. I'm not going to quote again all the books written by generals, by foreign generals, on the topic which confirm my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the last question I'm going to put to you during this examination, Colonel Barriot: What is your general conclusion on the basis of your experience?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I completely fail to understand how a question like that can be of any value to this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Quite so, Mr. Milosevic. Ask another question. That question is -- just doesn't make any sense at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Barriot. I have concluded my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I was handed over from you a bundle of documents which I guess you'd like to present as evidence. However, among them you dealt with only two tabs of it. Can I take it as you are going to present only two of them as evidence? Am I right in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have in mind the fact that these documents are self-explanatory, because these documents confirm the presence of the witness at the sites that he spoke of, testified about. It seems to me that no comment is necessary. Therefore, I ask that all these exhibits be admitted into evidence although I did not invoke many of them because many of them just have to do with establishing the presence of the witness at certain particular sites, and also the references that are taken as a basis for his competence. I should like to draw your attention to the following: As for both witnesses, the tabs coincide. I have sent a note to that effect. So therefore, what I ask for is that they all be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even so, no, speaking for myself, I don't think it is a proper way to present the written documents as evidence. Unless it is put to the witness I'm not inclined to admit any of them. So even if it is time-consuming, you have to put every document to the witness in order to introduce them as evidence. So if there's any documents that you'd like to produce other than tabs 4 and 27, you have to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, with all due respect for what you've said just now and which is, in principle, correct, and I'm not denying that, I think that the documents are self-explanatory. Look, for example, at the letter of the chief of police. The -- I'm dealing with them in order. Now I've -- well, you've got only the front page of the book, but Mrs. Del Ponte said yesterday that she had read these books. Then you have a certificate that was signed by General de Lapresle in relation to the UNPROFOR medal that was conferred upon Mr. Barriot. Then the letter of Milan Martic under number 4. And then number 5 is the certificate of Air Travel Croatia. And then number 6 is certificate of employment as medical staff at Glina Hospital. And then number 7 is report -- and so on and so forth. All of these are documents. I did not want to waste time introducing each and every one of them through the witness and showing them to the witness and so on. These are documents that have their own headings, their substance, their content, and they attest to the presence of the witness in the area and all the knowledge he could have gained while in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in the Prosecution case, your practice was to simply refer to them and then you had a number of tabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think typically -- I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Even if you didn't put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Typically documents will be dealt with individually. From time to time, documents were dealt with compendiously, but their being dealt with in that way was always explained and a foundation for their being produced in that way was laid with the witness. There are no doubt some exceptions to the general rule and we know there were some other exhibits that were produced, for example, collections of exhibits that were produced on the basis of production through, for example, compulsion to the state concerned and then commentary by the OTP in the form of a filing. Our position, as advanced in the recent filing that's been made available to the accused and that I hope he has read, as he must do if he's going to conduct the case as if counsel, is that that's the practice that should now obtain and that only exhibits properly relied on or identified should burden the Trial Chamber, and indeed the OTP, from this stage onwards. Now, in relation to this particular witness, that would mean that only the two tabs should be produced, and the accused will not be inconvenienced by this, because if -- because he's been able to adduce the evidence, either as to generality or detail, without reference to these documents. If the detail is challenged, it will be open to him in re-examination to say, for example, well, it's been challenged that you weren't present at X, Y, and Z on this particular date; do you now produce this document? By this method we will keep to the necessary minimum the number of documents that burden the record. To allow documents to go in without being relied on or referred to is an inappropriate process and one we would resist. We should also observe that although we've been provided with translations more recently today - and Ms. Dicklich is correcting the record as I go along - there are still, I think, four, tabs 9, 11, 14, and 17, that either are not translated or for which we have yet to be provided with translations, and many of the others that were translated have been translated only recently so that it hasn't been possible for us to give any particularly detailed consideration to them. So in our submission just the two tabs, maybe more in re-examination if they become relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice, you are, of course, right that the documents should be produced through the witness, but in the interests of fairness to the accused and in view of the approach that I knew you took in some cases, I'm going to allow the accused - Mr. Milosevic, listen Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond carefully - to just go through very quickly with the witness each tab, just to cite to the witness the title, and he can just say yes or no. The Prosecutor did that, so we'll allow you to do the same.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you have this set of documents in front of you. Do you have all the tabs as presented? Now you do have it before you. So number 1 is the front page of the book, The Assassination of a People. Is that your book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just say yes or no, please. Then number 2 is Our Testimony on Serbia. Again, is that your book?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Three, certificate signed by General Lapresle awarding the UNPROFOR medal to you. Is that a document that confirms that fact?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then number 4, decision signed by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's been dealt with. Go to number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Number 5, certificate of air travel in Croatia, 1994. Is that yours?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Number 6, certificate of employment as medical staff of Glina Hospital. Seven -- is that all right? Eight, medical work performed at Glina Hospital. That was number 8. So there were these two reports. Are both yours?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Number 9, letter of acknowledgement for assistance rendered at Glina Hospital. Number 10 also. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Eleven, report on travel in Krajina forwarded by Association Krajina, humanitarian association. Twelve also. Thirteen, Topusko hotel invoice; 14, [In English] Report on travel in Bosnia and Krajina in June 1995; 15 accreditation for reporting purposes provided by the Republika Srpska of Bosnia to a team of journalists of French TV channel FR3 in 1995 and 1996; 16, authorisation to participate in the Vidovdan ceremonies in Bijeljina, in 1995; 17, text written by General Mladic, Bijeljina, June 1995. Then Banja Luka hotel invoice, March 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pausing there. Let's go to number 17. Is that handwriting by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He wrote that for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he did. I can confirm this. He wrote it for me in June 1995 in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The dedication says, "For peace and friendship, I would like for France to think of us the way we think of it." Then there's a signature and then the 28th of June, 1995. Is that right? Okay. All right. I've already gone through the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. If we go back to number 14. We have text only in B/C/S, but you confirm this. You understand the Serbian language or you can read this? What is this? If you could tell us what this is. Number 14.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have in mind the text by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Number 14 is certificate on travel, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not speak or I don't understand the Cyrillic alphabet, but I know what it is about. I know the dates and the circumstances of the travel, especially with the passports and the number plates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Eighteen and 19 we've dealt with already. Twenty is Pristina, a hotel invoice too. Then 21, text by Rector Papovic, who you refer to, 1998. Twenty-two is letter of recommendation by [In English] His Grace Luka, Bishop of Western Europe for a mission in Kosovo. [Interpretation] Then 23, mission letter for Kosovo issued by Patriarch Pavle in June 1998. Then 24, [In English] Confirmation of presence in Kosovo issued by the Pec police in August 1998. [Interpretation] Twenty-five --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness should be indicating yes or no to these.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's nodding his head. Yes, I mean, we are saving time a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then tab 25, [In English] Letter of acknowledgement from Patriarch Pavle on receipt of a text on Krajina; 26, letter from French national TV channel antenna 2 on the release of French hostages; 27, Ministry of Civil Affairs and Communications section for relations with Interpol. [Interpretation] That is what we quoted from. That was not challenged in any way. Then 28 is a CD-ROM film, The Unit of El Mujahedin; and 29, photographs of terrorists. That's all we have there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand what the CD-ROM is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You don't have to admit that because we haven't shown it. So this was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't have 29 either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you don't have it. You don't have it. I don't have it either. I just have it on my list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noticed --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now we've gone through all of this, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice was on foot, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was only on foot to say we don't have the CD-ROM either and we know nothing about it, nor the following photographs either. As to the first two tabs, of course they are only the cover sheets of the documents concerned and that's all that's being admitted, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Well, we'll admit these documents as -- what's the next number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: D270. D270. Well, that's your examination-in-chief, so we move now to the cross-examination. Madam Prosecutor. MS. DEL PONTE: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Barriot, first of all you call Mr. Milosevic "Mr. President." Can you tell me why, because you know he is no longer president. He has not been a president for many years now.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a rule in France. You always call somebody "President" when that somebody has been the president of a republic, out of respect. It's just out of courtesy, French courtesy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: What is your current job?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm presently a specialist doctor for hospitals and I do lecture in several schools of medicine and in various ecoles speciales, specialised schools, and I'm part of an expert group working on weapon systems and terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: But you're also a doctor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My initial speciality is anaesthetics and emergency care, so I currently practice as an anaesthesiologist and also for primary care, emergency care.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about the job that you had as the official representative of the Serbian Republic of Krajina. You opened that office in Paris, and you showed in the documents the decision by President Milan Martic to this effect. What I'm interested in is the following: Why did you want to open this office? Did you think of this yourself or was the idea from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a joint idea. It emerged at the same time. I made the proposal and it was accepted by President Milan Martic and by his advisors. So it can be said that this was a joint project which gradually emerged. It didn't come about in June 1995, it took several months to come about in 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: So through the links of personal friendships you had President Martic, through discussions with him, that's how the idea came about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: And how long did it exist, this office?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was officially inaugurated in June 1994 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1995, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but it never closed. It's true that as of August 1995, because Krajina had been invaded by the Croatian forces, therefore it was not really possible any longer to maintain a representation of the RSK as such, but I remained a representative of the Krajina Serbs, especially in Bosnia and Kosovo, in order to maintain the representation and to keep looking after the RSK Serb refugees, especially in Kosovo. When I met with Karadzic and Mladic, I represented the Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Did you have any trouble with the French government? If I understood you properly yesterday, you said that this was the reason why you gave up your military career in the French army.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was punished by the minister of defence, Jean Chevenement, at the time, and Mate Granic lodged a complaint, the Croatian foreign affairs minister, so I was arrested for several days. I was criticised, but it was because I did not comply with the duty of silence.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: That we've known since yesterday.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not because I failed to respect the army or because of any non-compliance or for lies, it was only because I had told the truth, but the truth should not have been told.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You were in the former Yugoslavia as a doctor for the UNPROFOR. That was your official position, and that lasted three months. That's right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: But as to the other visits you paid, two-, three-week-long visits every two or three months, that was on a private basis?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was as a private individual. I was no longer within the UNPROFOR. It was as a part of a humanitarian organisation, basically the Krajina humanitarian organisation funded by Bucan and Teleobjectif founded by Marica Mathei.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: So you were interested in the former Yugoslavia and facts relating to it as early as in 1994?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Because before you were not interested?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only experience I had in the Balkans before that was a mission to Albania in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: In 1991. And who for?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Tirana when there was some kind of an insurrection in Tirana. So I had been dispatched to foreign embassies, and I was the only Western doctor present then, and I looked after the Albanian insurgents that had sought refuge in various foreign embassies. There were many thousands of them. I looked after them for several weeks, and I took some of them, several back to France. Several thousands of them were welcomed back in France.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: It can be said that as to the facts mentioned in the indictment against Milosevic regarding Croatia for the periods of 1991, 1992, you were not on the ground.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just made a mistake regarding the date of my mission to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yes. We do have the relevant documents we were provided with.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in 1990, July.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Right. July 1990.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I can see that. So '80, '82 you were in Paris, '90 you were in Albania and you were in Iraq in '91.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: In other words, you were not present at the time of the Croatian indictment against Milosevic. You were not in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Just for my own sake and for the Judges' sake, can you tell me this: We heard Ms. Eve Crepin, but I saw in the Belgrade press from this morning that you are apparently married. Can you explain the kind of relationship you have with Ms. or Mrs. Crepin.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We live together but we're not married.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: How long have you been living together?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yesterday in your testimony, today also, you testified to, let's say, Muslim terrorism and mainly in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You mentioned names of possible authors or perpetrators of attacks, but of course your testimony is a mere assessment by you of what you learned speaking to various people. What I'm asking you, what the Judges asked you yesterday was this: Do you have any document to support what you say?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, madam, no doubt that as soon as you mention sensitive areas such as the topic of terrorism, most of the sources are classified as secret, and a French individual is not allowed to mention classified information. So whenever I was in a position to present to you a source or a document that was not classified as secret by the French authorities, for instance, this exhibit, the Ministry of Civil Affairs regarding the presence of Mr. Mohammed Atta, I did, in the same way a DVD was mentioned which is not going to be produced where you see Mr. Halzaouari together with Mr. Izetbegovic in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So in some cases I was able to produce evidence. In other instances, these are official sources that provided me with the information but I'm not authorised to mention them because these are classified secret documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: But you agree with me anybody can come here, can state anything and ask for it to be tendered into evidence whilst it is not evidence for me. I mean, it could be your private opinion, your private assessment of what you may know.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You then questioned the positions I had and what I may have done in my life. I gave you a very simple example. I'm sorry -- sorry for the interpreters. Yes, I gave you a very -- I can give you a very simple example. I was planning to bring here the list of French soldiers or French Blue Helmets who were killed in Bosnia, 56 of them to be precise. More than two-thirds were killed by Muslim sniper fire, and I asked to be allowed to introduce this list to the French military authorities and this was refused because this is a classified, secret piece of information. Now, do you challenge the fact that 56 soldiers were killed in Bosnia until 1994, that two-thirds of them were killed by Muslim Bosnian fire? That's the truth. But I'm not authorised to present this to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you. You are now talking about terrorist acts by Muslims in Bosnia. That's not enough. It's not enough to just mention that. It's not enough to say this. I want to know precisely because that interests me too. Can you prove this? Just let me come back to this document you produced regarding the 9/11 events. You said that the French authorities had allowed you to produce this document. What can I see, however, on this document? I can see this document was sent to you by fax by the Presidency of Republika Srpska. You can see "Presi BH." I suppose that's Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see where it comes from, but look at the people it is directed to. How can you not know that this was sent to the French intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I ask you this question because I know perfectly well that the French authorities do not authorise any document to be produced, not a single one of this kind. Of course I have not had time to check this with the French authorities, but I can see that this comes from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, but you're distorting what I said. I never said that the French authorities had allowed me. I said that they did not forbid this, and when it is part of a French document such as the list of the French Blue Helmets killed, the French authorities can say no because these are French documents, but inasmuch as these documents were channeled to me by other sources and are not French documents, there is no reason whatsoever for not allowing me to produce them.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Who did you seek the approval of - I mean, from the French authorities - to produce this document? I'd like to check this, you see. Can you give me a name, be it only one?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't give you any single name.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Which office or servants?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that this comes from the Military Intelligence Service, but I can't tell you which service or department, but it's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: But it's not even a classified document.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're distorting the issue or dodging the issue. The problem is that this document shows that Mr. Mohammed Atta was in Bosnia in 1999. So either you challenge his presence --

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I do not challenge his presence. I'm trying to ascertain how you got hold of the document. If you tell me that you have been authorised by this intelligence department from the French military authorities, okay, but I would say that it amazes me because that's not what they usually do. And I tell you in addition to that that this has not been classified as a secret document by France. But never mind. I don't want to delve into this because, well, the fact Atta was there does not change anything to our discussions, not an iota. I can produce any document showing that Mr. Atta was in Zurich and that's not a reason for claiming that Switzerland was involved in terrorist acts. But let's go back to snipers in Sarajevo. We know that and the Judges, the Trial Chamber knows that as well. That was true for all the sides in the conflict. There were people who were snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... speech that's being made.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this is a completely inappropriate comparison, because the village of Bakotic, I showed you a film at Maglaj, a review of the Mujahedin Brigade. There are no air links between Bakotic and America but there are between Zurich and America. So Atta, when he went from Bosnia, he had to go somewhere in Europe to fly on from there, so you can't compare Maglaj and the village of Bakotic with Zurich and the reasons for his stay in Zurich or Bakotic or elsewhere. He wasn't in Bakotic for the same reasons that he was in Zurich for quite certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I'd ask you not to indulge in comments and to confine your questions to fact situations. What is the precise question that you're asking? MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: The precise question runs as follows: Dr. Barriot, do you know anything about the Vrbanja incident in Sarajevo in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember it very clearly, but if I remember correctly, it was a clash between French soldiers and the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And there were casualties. How many people died?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few people died. Two or three, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yes. This is to say that Serbs killed people because you said that the French Blue Helmets had been killed by snipers. The Vrbanja bridge incident led to a number of deaths.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't compare this. Something had been planned. I can quote or mention French soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Barriot. You said that MacKenzie, didn't you, MacKenzie stressed that it was the Muslims, and you talked about the long queue. I have MacKenzie's book here at hand. I don't want to adduce it as evidence, but I'd like to -- on a particular page General MacKenzie says, and I'm sure you will agree with me, Dr. Barriot, that he expresses doubt, but he does not adopt a categorical attitude vis-a-vis the situation, in particular with the -- what you quoted, the 27th of May disaster in Sarajevo. [In English] "Attacked and at least 17 killed." [Interpretation] That is the passage you quoted, isn't it? And he says, [In English] "... it was a set-up using explosives. Our people tell us there were a number of things that didn't fit. The street had been blocked off just before the incident. ... The majority of people killed are alleged to be 'tame Serbs.' Who knows?" -- [Interpretation] says -- "Who knows," says General MacKenzie. Do you agree with me here, Dr. Barriot? Do you agree with me? I would like your answer.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to answer. The street had been cut off been on both sides by the Bosnian authorities just before the attack. Once the people were lined up before the bakery, the media came to the forefront but stayed behind, and that's when the attack started. I don't know if you understand ballistics, but I would like you to explain to me how a mortar shot at that distance could possibly reach a queue, a line of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I wanted you to tell me General MacKenzie, I just wanted to check that you quoted the same passage which I read out in English, that General MacKenzie is saying "Who knows"; in other words, the perpetrators of this attack, who knows who the perpetrators are. The question remains unanswered. It's an open question.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as the book is concerned, yes, but afterwards he made statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yes, well, I shall stick to the book.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you intend to call about Markale 1 and Markale 2 so that we are more precise on this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: General Rose never mentioned Markale. As you know, there must be some documents. We need evidence. It's not possible that somebody turns up here and just states something.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do like you do. I -- I --

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I have a book at hand here.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a number of references and books and articles that are all dated, and I can provide these likewise.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you a number of questions about the situation in Croatia. Let's first of all talk about 1991, the events in 1991. You, in your deposition, talked about the crimes committed by the Croats in 1991, described these in great detail, and you stressed that no crimes had been committed by the Serbs and that the latter launched -- only launched operation in the last months of 1991. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are distorting what I said. I will not corroborate this. I never said that crimes were never committed on both sides. This is not what I said. I never challenged that. During a civil war crimes are obviously committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You were not that clear-cut yesterday but I'm listening with great interest to what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is attacks against the Serbs had been planned since 1990 and the instruments in all of this had been set up beforehand by the Ministry of the Interior and the National Guard units that were being -- had been created to attack the Serbs. This is what I said. I said that the Serbs fought primarily during the second half of the year and that they had fought in Krajina, but they had not fought outside their -- in Zagreb Rijeka, in other words, outside their own territories.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: In other words, you saying quite clearly today that you admit that the Serbs have also committed crimes during that same period of time. Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote down on paper that Serbians are not angels either and that they may -- I would like to quote this. I would like to quote my book. When we're dealing with a civil war, it's out of the question to say that one of the parties to the conflict has not committed a single crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You are not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Fine. We had somebody testifying here, Mr. Milan Babic. You know who Mr. Milan Babic is?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do. He was the first president of Croatia before Goran Hadzic and before Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: That's quite right. So he testified here and I'm not going to read out his testimony for the acts in question. 27 November 2002, 13064 and 066 is the transcript page number. I shall sum all of this up in one single sentence. Milan Babic says that the crimes committed by local Serbs together with the JNA were committed against non-Serbs in Krajina, and more -- and particularly to force the Serbs to flee these regions. Do you admit to this, to the non-Serbs to flee the region? This is how you understand it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Milan Babic can say what he likes. All I can say is what I've seen in 1994, in other words in Krajina there were tens of thousands of Muslims and there were also Croatian people in the Glina Hospital. There were Croatians who wanted to stay and live in peace with the Serbs in Krajina, and nobody drove them out. And I'm just talking to you about what I experienced. Tens of thousands of Muslims in Krajina, in other words, non-Serbs. I also saw Croatian people who, if they wanted to stay, could stay and were now threatened. This is what I actually saw. So Mr. Milan Babic of course is -- can only be held responsible for what he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Yes. You were there, and in 1994 -- 1914 you were --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not born in 1914.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: 1994. 1994, but you weren't there in 1991 so you -- you cannot testify --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this emphasis on the fact that the witness wasn't there in 1991 is tendentious. We're not disputing that he wasn't there in 1991, but yesterday we had established precisely that the witness attended more than ten briefings at UNPROFOR where they professionally analysed all the events that took place since UNPROFOR began its mission, that is to say in 1991 and 1992 and 1993. We established that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Prosecutor is entitled to put that to the witness. It's for us to evaluate the evidence. There's nothing improper in that. It's time for the break, Madam Prosecutor. We'll break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Prosecutor. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Dr. Barriot, do you know anything about the crimes which were committed by the Serb forces in the following regions: I am mentioning this because these are all mentioned in the indictment. Milosevic is charged with these crimes that were committed in Dalmatia in the Lika area, Banja area, Western Slavonia, Eastern Slavonia, and Vukovar in particular Erdut, Lovas. Do you know or are you aware of these facts?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have just quoted place names but you haven't given me any dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: This is still in 1991, from August 1991 to November -- December 1991.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, given the dates you have quoted, you talk about the second half of 1991, and the Serb territories in Croatia I am aware of primarily what the Tomislav Mercep and Abramovic Croatian militia have done, but I'm not aware of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Committed by the paramilitary Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the primary attacks by the Croatians and legitimate self-defence by the Serbs who were not prepared to be killed without defending themselves. I'm not aware of any crimes primarily committed or first of all committed by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You have rather a selective memory, I dare say.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Whatever the case may be, I would like to show you a document, Exhibit 342, tab 11. This is the report written by a high-ranking officer in the JNA, Lieutenant Colonel Eremija, who is the commander, the deputy commander for political affairs and morale in the 1st Division of the Mechanised Guard of the JNA. This document is dated 24th of October, 1991 -- 23rd of October -- 3rd of October, and was talking about his unit -- 23rd of October and was talking about his unit which was active in Western Slavonia at the time. I should like to draw your attention to the following: Page 2, at the bottom of the page 2, and page 3, the top of the page and paragraph 5 on page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the document please be placed on the ELMO. Thank you. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: My question is as follows: You are aware of the letter and its contents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, just a moment. MS. DEL PONTE: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could the document be placed on the ELMO. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: So my question -- well, as you've just read the passage, have you, Dr. Barriot? So I would like to know whether you're aware of this letter and its content, because this letter had been published in the international press a few months later.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question, I have never read this entire letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: You agree with me, and you -- do you agree that the Colonel Eremija admits that the Serbs had committed crimes, crimes in Western Slavonia in the autumn of 1991? There is no doubt about that when you read these passages I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with the way in which you present this to me. There was never any question of denying the fact that there was fighting. This was the second half of the year 1991. This was a period in time when there was fighting in the Krajina. This started at Gospic in September of 1991 and then in Slavonia and Western Slavonia, Pakracka Poljana in October and then in Eastern Slavonia and Prijedor. So -- that there was fighting. I repeat I think nobody can deny this, but the point on which I would like to labour is that the fighting was due to response to the MUP and the National Guard, which was Croatian. That there was fighting and casualties on both sides I don't think is questionable.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: This is the way you interpret this. I think we shall let the Judges rule on this. This just demonstrates that there were Serb paramilitary forces that did commit crimes. Let's now move on to UNPROFOR. You said that you were kept abreast of what had happened in 1991 and in the following years. I have here in front of me a report written by the Secretary-General of the United Nations Security Council, and I would like this document to be tendered into evidence. You testified about the fact that you forge your opinion based on the fact what had happened in 1992, 1993, and you base this on what you had heard from your colleagues working for UNPROFOR. The document which I'm about to show you and ask you to read indicates a number of things, and indicates, Dr. Barriot, that you were not well-informed or fully informed about the facts. Now, let's look at the following paragraphs in detail: Paragraph 2, which talks about, amongst other things, the Croatian attack in the Miljevci plateau area, and paragraph 3, which mentions other attacks by the Croatian forces. I would like now to draw your attention to paragraph 4, more specifically, in other words, the creation of a new police force which is Serb in order to bypass the Vance Plan. The commander of UNPROFOR considers that these forces are paramilitary forces. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: And in paragraph 6, the word "terrorism" is used. This term "terrorism" is spelled out in paragraph 10 to 17, and more importantly and which I would like to stress here, we are talking about harassment of non-Serb minorities living in the territories controlled by the Serbs in Croatia. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't confirm anything at all. You are showing me a document which I know nothing about. I agree you are mentioning the Miljevaca plateau in June of 1994.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, yes. So we can agree that in 1992, the Serb territorial forces in June 1992 were aggressed or attacked by the Croatian forces. There were four people dead among the Serb territorial forces. The bodies were thrown in a well. I was in the San Salva hospital [phoen] in Knin, and I met the forensic doctors because the -- in the summer of 1992, we were unable to put the pieces together. This was a most terrible massacre, and Janko Dzerenko [phoen] was there on the spot, and then a UN Resolution asked the Croatian forces to move out of the Miljevaca plateau and they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, what I would like to underline here is the fact that UNPROFOR has, via the Secretary-General, produced a document and also mentions harassment of non-Serb minorities living in the territories controlled by the Serbs in Croatia, because you are saying that the Serbs in this particular territory are only victims or are just in a position of legitimate self-defence, whereas UNPROFOR, which provided you with all the data in 1994, drafts a report which is totally independent, whereas you are not.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. You are distorting the facts totally. You are talking about the events in 1992, whereas I said on several occasions, and that cannot be challenged, the attack on Serbs started in 1990 and 1991, and after all the events in 1991 - I can quote them all - everything that happened in that region; Northern Dalmatia, Kopinj [phoen] area, but I answer, if I may, where the troops from Makunerac [phoen] massacred Serbs, Tiro [phoen], Meskovic [phoen], all this happened in this region. You're now telling me that the Serbs were defending themselves. This was not harassment, this was just a question of legitimate self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Fine. We shall now move on to the observations made by the UN Secretary-General in paragraph 33 to 34, where he states -- I would like to draw your attention to this paragraph, paragraph 34, which mentions the responsibility of the Serbs in Krajina for the deterioration of the situation in Krajina. And in paragraph 35, the UN Secretary-General explains the frustration of the Croat authorities in the light of this situation and describes it as something which is totally incomprehensible. This is what I would like to draw your attention to.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. We are talking about 1992, and you totally overlook the fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Doctor, you don't agree -- Barriot, you don't agree with this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with the interpretation of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: This is not a question of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I have a very clear question to put to you after all that. Dr. Barriot, is it not right to say that the fact that the Serbs in Krajina refused to abide by the Vance Plan and that they refused to adopt a peaceful solution meant that the Z-4 plan was also rejected? This encouraged the Croats to adopt a military position to try and find a settlement to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with this interpretation, because if we go back to 1991, 1992, 1993, the attacks and the plan which you've just mentioned, the Zagreb 4 plan came under -- came after a number of years where massacres were being perpetrated against the Serbs and the Zagreb 4 failed is because Franjo Tudjman did not want to discuss the matter with Martic and Martic was on the list of war criminals. This was not that the Serbs were unwilling to accept this, they were not provided with the possibility of negotiating this or finding a solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: This is the way you see things. We have a number of documents, a number of testimony, and we also have Ambassador Galbraith's testimony on this point. Now, let me move on to another subject. You mentioned yesterday that the Serbs in Krajina no longer had heavy weaponry after 1992. So if we are to look at the letter which commander of the UNPROFOR, General Lars Wahlgren sent on the 1st of April, 1993, to Goran Hadzic, president of RSK. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] This, Your Honour, is a new document which I would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the number will be 815. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] We should also have a number for the Security Council report that I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that is the Security Council report of the 28th September? MS. DEL PONTE: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's 815, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just an observation on that: Of course it wasn't a document adopted by the witness, so -- we've been studying the filing by the Prosecution on exhibits in this case where they complain about documents being put into evidence that are not adopted or referred to and taken no further, and don't we have an example of it with this document of the 28th of September, 1992? She's been putting cross-examination, but the witness hasn't been able to comment about it. He says he's unfamiliar with it -- MS. DEL PONTE: No, he comments. He interpret. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think we can apply those strict common law rules to admission of documents here. This system is a little different. The UN document is -- MS. DEL PONTE: Public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a public document in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, assist me if you can, please. This is a document which hasn't been part of the Prosecution case so far. MS. DEL PONTE: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This witness has -- has made it clear he knows nothing about it. So if it's admitted, what's its status? MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Of course this document is in contradiction to everything the witness says on this topic, because here you have a report by the commander, the general command -- by General Nambiar, who was the UNPROFOR commander in 1992. And this is a report in relation to the situation in Croatia. The witness mentioned the situation. This contradicts everything he said. So it is important for me to get a comment from the witness, for him to look at this document. I wanted to ask him to comment on it, because I think this is a very relevant document. Indeed, what he said yesterday and today is to be found in this document, and this is in contradiction to what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may well be relevant, but my concern is how does it acquire a status in the case when the witness hasn't accepted any part of it, it's not presented as part of the Prosecution case, although it could have been if it was thought to have been important. It could perhaps be produced at a later stage in the case when the opportunity does arise to seek to answer part of the Defence case. But I just want to be clear, in case there's a series of these, that the decision we make is on solid ground. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honour, that I presented this document to the witness, and I asked him to comment on it, because this denies the witness statement. So I think that document may be produced now since it is being used now, here at the hearing. What the witness has just said prompts me to say that I have a report by the UNPROFOR commander. He says that he got this information from meetings he had with the UNPROFOR, but you have here the UNPROFOR commander drafting a report conveyed to the UN Secretary-General. That's the reason why this should be produced now and tendered into evidence, because I am now presenting this document for assessment by the witness. He's discussed this. Even if he hasn't seen it before, he's seen it now and he's discussing it, so I think now is the time for the document to be tendered into evidence. That's my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this explanation given in response to Mr. Bonomy's question, the one provided by Ms. Del Ponte, her main assertion is that the document is contradictory to the testimony of this witness. That explanation is not correct. If you look at the document - this is also the first time that I see it - you will see that it starts with the following -- look at the first chapter, and it says: "[In English] However, tension has been high in Sector South, particularly in the areas of Peruca dam, Miljevci plateau (where there was a Croatian army incursion on 21st of June, 1992) ..." [Interpretation] And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you looking at the same document? What paragraph of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've quoted it. It's on page 1, paragraph 2, and it refers to the merit of the case. [In English] "The major incidents that have generated considerable tension have been as follows:" [Interpretation] And (a): "[In English] On 7 August 1992, fighting erupted in an area adjacent to the south-eastern portion of Sector West, apparently due to attempts by armed elements from the Croatian side to cross the Sava River and attack Bosnian Serb elements south of the river."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... presenting it as a document that contradicts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can I make an observation? I think we are having a useless debate. I noted, just noted this exhibit was exhibited already by the Defence. Its number is D93. So it is already in the exhibit list, and I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if I can make further observation, the letter which is given the number 815 should be 814. The Road to War was not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wanted to say to Mr. Milosevic the Prosecutor is presenting it as a document that contradicts the testimony of the witness. The extent to which it achieves that purpose, the extent to which it does that is a matter for us to determine. So the fact that you can point to passages in the document which are not a contradiction doesn't go to the admissibility. It goes to the weight. But in any event, the document is already tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it may be that we disagree about this. I find difficulty with the concept in an adversarial system that the Prosecution can positively introduce material that is not accepted by the witness, the Defence witness who is giving evidence at that time, and therefore I'm exploring the proper legal basis on which this can become a positive part of the Prosecution case. Now, that's a matter that we can debate later, because as it turns out, this is a Defence production, and it my opinion it should not have a Prosecution exhibit number. MS. DEL PONTE: Even if it is -- sorry. Even if it is a public document that I use for the cross-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is my opinion at the moment. And I don't think it's necessary to reach a final conclusion. It's sufficient that it has a D93 number for present purposes, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Madam Prosecutor. MS. DEL PONTE: Yes. We have the second document. That is the letter, the Hadzic -- letter to Hadzic. That is -- [Interpretation] since the witness said that the Krajina Serbs no longer had any heavy weaponry after 1992, I'm seeking to tender this letter into evidence. This is a letter by General Lars Wahlgren, UNPROFOR commander. It was sent to Goran Hadzic on the 1st of April, 1993. Hadzic was then president of the RSK. Now, as to the motives. This shows several examples of heavy weaponry fire by Krajina Serbs on civilian -- Croatian civilian targets in March 1993. Note page 3. You have a survey of the weapons used. Under 4 it is even mentioned that on the 11th of March, 1993, six cluster bombs were used in Sibenik. The witness mentioned cluster bombs used by the other side, according to him, in Kosovo, and of the, of course, negative effects they had. So I'm tendering this letter. I'd like this letter to be submitted to the witness for him to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Point him to the specific passage on which he is to comment. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Second paragraph, Your Honour, and page 3 as to the types of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd say two things regarding this document that I've never seen before. I'm therefore discovering it now. Regarding the last but one document, you said that this contradicts what I said. Sorry, it does not contradict it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. You do not -- you do not determine the rules here. We are past that. We are now dealing with the letter addressed to Mr. Hadzic, and the Prosecutor wants you to comment on the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My comment refers to documents going back to 1992 and 1993, and I stated very clearly that all the documents that I had analysing the UNPROFOR back in 1994 went from 1990 to 1994, including, therefore, events that happened after the production of these two documents. It cannot be said that the analysis I had provided of UNPROFOR in 1994 would be contradicted by documents that happened before, in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, you're bordering on being out of order and contemptuous. You really are. You're skating on very thin ice. I've already told you that is ground we have already covered. We are not returning do it. Address yourself now exclusively to the specific question put by the Prosecutor. The second paragraph of the letter. Do you have it there? Do you have the letter in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Second paragraph. Madam Prosecutor, it's the second paragraph, the one beginning, "As you are no doubt aware ..." MS. DEL PONTE: Yes, particularly the second paragraph. The first also, but -- [Interpretation] the information I'm seeking from the witness is this: He said that there were no heavy weaponry, and I say this letter shows that there was heavy weaponry and even cluster bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Therefore I'm asking the witness whether he admits that he had only partial information.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't agree with that, because when I mentioned heavy weaponry, I think of tanks, of planes. I'm not having in mind rockets or rocket launchers which can be moved about very quickly and which, unlike truly heavy weaponry, can be moved whilst the latter cannot. And I also observe that this is in April 1993. So then Serbs were trying to respond to aggressions and attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Colonel Barriot, what I understand this question to be asking you to consider is whether you accept that in the light of the second paragraph of this letter and the fourth item on the third page, that it's possible that weapons were improperly used against civilian persons by Serb forces based in Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. -- there are two different things I'm forced to admit because I have no reason to question what an UNPROFOR general would say. I admit that there was firing with these weapons. As to know why, that's a matter for interpretation and it doesn't show that this fire was directed at civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you accept that it's possible that this is an accurate report? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes. You're addressing a question to Judge Bonomy?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He raised the issue. Mrs. Del Ponte says that the witness had partial information when he testified, and on the other hand, Mrs. Del Ponte is also using partial information. When it is not compared to the other side, it doesn't mean a thing. I would like to draw your attention to the last paragraph of this letter, and it reads as follows: I am writing to the other party to this conflict --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, I've stopped you because, as I have told you on a number of occasions, a matter like that is classically an issue to be taken up in re-examination. When you re-examine, you simply draw the attention of the witness to the third paragraph and read it to him or ask him to read it, but you don't interrupt to make the point now. Yes. Please continue. MS. DEL PONTE: We can continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic, Dr. Barriot, namely the support by the US air force during the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You would like to exhibit this? MS. DEL PONTE: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And Judge Kwon can assure us that it is not already a Defence or Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 814, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just explain that I see a difference between the situation of this document and the situation of the previous one because this witness, as a Defence witness, has accepted that it's possible that this is an accurate report and that it thus becomes part of the case that the Prosecutor can rely on at a later stage. MS. DEL PONTE: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Oh. I thought it was on. Sorry. I have -- we have information gathered by Human Rights Watch, and it makes it possible to have a better understanding of what happened. Here again, we have a document dated August 1996 from Human Rights Watch, and I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: On page 8 it is said, and let me quote this passage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do we have the document, Madam Prosecutor? MS. DEL PONTE: Oh, yes. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Doctor, please take page 8, the first paragraph -- the first full paragraph of this page. It says, and I quote: "[In English] NATO threatened to attack Croatian forces in retaliation for their assault on UN positions. However, the only NATO attack during the operation was against a Serbian surface-to-air missile site near Knin that had locked onto two NATO planes dispatched in response to UN calls for support." [Interpretation] Were you aware of this? Were you aware of these facts?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My response, my answer will be very simple. You mention attacks by US air force onto batteries --

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: No. These are NATO, not US attacks.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: But when the 19 ambassadors, NATO ambassadors are the only one accredited to allow army intervention, when did they sign this order for operation on Knin? This is no such document. There was no NATO order to launch an attack on Knin. It is the US army.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: We're not talking about the US army.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, it is the US army that bombed the Ogdina [phoen] airport in Krajina, and it is again that same army which attacked defensive or defence arms. These arms used by the Serbs were aimed at defending Knin, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: It is up for the Trial Chamber to adjudicate this. I read a document, and I can read in this that this was an attack by NATO. I don't deny that there may have been American aeroplanes, but this is NATO.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This comes from Human Rights Watch, and I don't think that they are able to provide this type of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I do work with the documents I have, Doctor. And here I can read that this is upon -- upon a request by the UN that NATO attacked.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This comes from Human Rights Watch. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Can I tender this document into evidence, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be 815.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've got the same running objection, so to speak, in a document that's not adopted by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think the witness agrees with this paragraph, apart from the issue whether it was NATO or the United States which attacked Knin. This paragraph is dealing with the abuse by Croatian government, and I remember the witness said yes to the answer of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I took it that there was a disavowal by him and that they'd descended into an argument over whether it was UN or NATO and whether who was performing what rather than the content of the document which was meant -- which is really designed to show that it was the Serbs who were on the offensive and were being repelled and attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're saying that if the Prosecutor wants to introduce this, then they must introduce it in rebuttal through a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In rebuttal. We are in a danger here. It's something we've been observing over a succession of witnesses, and we're dealing with a response to the Prosecutor's current motion over material that's coming in that the witness looks at, well, there it is. But it's being put in as a vehicle, as a Trojan horse, if you like, for the Prosecutor into the Defence case, and the documents are not adopted by the witnesses so their actual worth is merely an assertion by counsel that they exist in the terms that they do when the witness himself has not adopted it, and it bears no impact on his testimony at all. If documents have already been in evidence, like the Kirudja document, D93, which we eventually found in the Defence documents, that of course is a different matter. But when we have documents that are being introduced for their own sake as a vehicle of expressing the case for the other side in a different form, I think the Trial Chamber is getting in a very dangerous area there because the document itself has no real status. It's not being produced by the witness. It's coming through the organ of the Prosecutor but without any foundation having been laid as to its merit, its provenance, what it means, how it arose, in the usual way, and if they are concerned with the number of exhibits that are piling up in the case, they seem to be not heeding their own alarm signals, if you like, and are adding considerably to them. But I suppose if it suits them, they're willing to go along with it; if it doesn't, they're not. I think we do need consistency in relation to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I consider this should be admitted, or exhibited, because there's sufficient in the answer, as indicated by Judge Kwon, to justify reference at least to that paragraph in the context of any later submissions. For that purpose alone, I support exhibiting this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further documents and just a few last questions so that we finish on time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Dr. Barriot, as regards Kosovo, you said that you were there in July of 1998 and for two weeks?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June for two weeks and July and August for one month.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Right. And you said that there were Albanians. You said that there were Albanian professionals in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: In the hospital. The accused Milosevic talks about paragraph 87 in the indictment that mentions facts in 1991. So as regards this, you don't know. You talked about 1998.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Fine. So as regards 1991, this remains to be seen. You talk about Kouchner. You attacked him personally here. As my colleague Mr. Nice said, we're not here to defend people, but Kouchner arrived much later, didn't he, after the facts mentioned in the indictment against Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. Mr. Kouchner was in Dubrovnik in 1991 and --

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: We're actually talking about Kosovo.
