utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kosovo. He arrived then.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Fine. One last point, and Mladic and Srebrenica. For a while I shuddered because you mentioned what Mladic had told you, which I can understand, because you know that there is an indictment against Mladic. You know this, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Do you know since when?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The indictment goes back to 1995, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Quite right. And you mentioned Oric. You do know that Oric is being prosecuted here? Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, recently so.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: But you know about this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Do you also know that a commission in the Republika Srpska was set up to look into the Srebrenica massacre?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, which is -- confirms what I've said.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Then we didn't read the same report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska commission admits that the Serb forces have massacred over 7.000 people in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I challenge that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: So you have not read this, but you know that Lord Ashdown set up this commission in Republika Srpska and they admitted publicly? This was a public admission.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what Lord Ashdown did for the Serb Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: But my question doesn't hinge on that. My question has to do with Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica I confirm what I've said already and I corroborate what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: This is what Mladic told you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think he was in the -- he knew full well and he knew much more about it than Paddy Ashdown. He was in the right position.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: He was also in a position to defend himself. So there are a number of things here in the evidence to state that there were 7 to 8.000 Muslim victims.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know full well as I do that there were 2.500 bodies which have been identified, 2.500 that were exhumed. So don't say that 10 years down the road there were 8.000, or sometimes it's been said 13.000 able-bodied men and that these are not women, children and elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Just one last question, Dr. Barriot: Do you admit that in this armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia crimes were committed on all sides?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told you that already.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Could you just confirm this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that from 1990 to 1999, there was a civil war in Yugoslavia, and there were casualties in the three communities.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I'm not talking about dead people, I'm talking about crimes committed by the various groups.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day in France you have crimes committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: I'm not talking to you about crimes committed in France. I'm asking you whether, yes or no, you agree with me that the fact that crimes were committed during this conflict by all the groups party to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, crimes were committed by the Muslims, by the Croats, by --

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] I've finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Colonel, can I ask you one question? Have I noted correctly that you have not read the report of the commission set up by Republika Srpska to investigate Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I read the reports. There were two reports, and we're not talking about the same one, the one which I believe was dictated by Paddy Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, can I ask this: I'd like to clarify what you answered to Judge Bonomy and Madam Prosecutor. When Madam Prosecutor asked you whether you had been allowed by the French government to disclose this document, I'm referring to tab 27 of your exhibit binder related to Mohammed Atta, if you remember, you said, I quote: "I did not say the French authorities allowed me." But when Judge Bonomy asked you how you came by with that document, you answered this way: "This was provided by intelligence services, and I was authorised to present them because they were not classified as secret by the French government." I'm a little bit confused. Could you elaborate on this matter.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Del Ponte did make a confusion here. I never said that the authorities had granted me permission to disclose these documents. I said that I had not been prohibited from doing so. Before coming here I wanted to show a number of documents. So the only one for which I was banned by the French authority was the list giving the names of the Blue Helmets who were killed in the former -- in Yugoslavia. But for the other documents I was told I was free to do what I liked but this was under my own responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Barriot, you're clearly a man committed to the Serbs, sympathetic to the Serbs, and for that one can have no quarrel. When did your association with Serbia begin? What was your first association? I know you went to Bosnia in 1993 with the Blue Helmets, I think, but what was the origin of your association, your relationship with Yugoslavia and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, after having served UNPROFOR and the Blue Helmets. It's after that time when I realised what was actually happening on the ground, I then got closer to the Serb people because I felt they were suffering from a great injustice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So your commitment arose as a result of what you saw in 1994.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is really what I experienced on the ground, what I heard, what I saw personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on now. Well, just a few linked to the document produced by Madam Del Ponte. I can't take the same order, take them in the same order but let me start off with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Barriot, look at the Human Rights Watch Helsinki document first, please. This is the first paragraph on page 8 which Madam Del Ponte quoted from. "[In English] During the offensive, Croatian forces restricted movement of most of the approximately 10.000 UN troops stationed in the Krajina area. They also attacked 65 UN posts, killing three and wounding eight peacekeepers during the offensive. NATO threatened to attack Croatian forces in retaliation for their assault on UN positions, however, the only NATO attack during the operation was against a Serbs surface-to-air missile ..." et cetera. [Interpretation] in Knin. Now, does that change anything with respect to your assertions and claims that it was American planes which attacked Knin?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It corroborates the fact that it was the US planes that fired on the positions around Knin. Also this corroborates the fact that the Croatian forces deliberately fired on the Blue Helmets and -- there is a Klaus Gomberger [phoen], a lieutenant officer who was deliberately killed by a Croat tank. Bernard Jean-Pierre [phoen] mentioned this, and a number of people were killed at the hands of the Croats during this attack. And Blue Helmets were used as human shields. And all the Blue Helmets, Canadian Blue Helmets who were thrown in gaol in Knin at the time that Knin town was being destroyed during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Milosevic. You said in answer to Mr. Milosevic that the paragraph that he read corroborates the fact that it was the US planes that fired on the positions around Knin. What is in that paragraph that corroborates that? In it I see no reference to the USA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the two planes, Your Honour, came from Teddy Roosevelt and they were two fighter planes. They were American fighter planes, and this is not challenged, and they fired on Knin. They were on an aircraft carrier. If I'm lying, it's easy to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it's not the paragraph itself that corroborates it, it's evidence which you have independently of the paragraph. Go ahead, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, Mr. Barriot, if you look at the end of the paragraph there's a footnote, because as Madam Del Ponte said, this is a document of the Human Rights Watch, but you have footnote number 14 indicated there, isn't that right? The very end of that paragraph, you have footnote 14.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, take a look at the bottom of the page what it says. What is footnote 14 and what is stated here? It says Raymond Bonner, so that's the article in The New York Times of the 5th of August, 1995, and the title is "[In English] In Broad Attack, Croatia Is Trying To Dislodge Serbs." [Interpretation] So that, therefore, is the article that appeared in The New York Times, to which this, as they say document of the Human Rights Watch is referring, and nothing more than that, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do corroborate that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look now quickly at this next point. Madam Del Ponte quoted General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A good point, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the quotation, as I was saying, of General MacKenzie, which is May the 27th, his diary, and that was what Madam Del Ponte was quoting from, briefly. I consider that it is necessary to read out that portion of the diary, but before I do that, I'd like to say that I had to look at the dictionary and find -- MacKenzie says this: "Tame Serbs" under quotation marks. "Tame." So what does "tame" mean? And I looked at the dictionary and read what it says: Domesticated, which means tamed. And now I can understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Pritonje" [phoen] would be the Serbian translation of the word tame, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let me read the following: "Disaster in Sarajevo. People lined up for bread. They were attacked and at least 17 killed. [In English] Presidency claims it was a Serb mortar attack. Serbs claim it was a set-up using explosives. Our people tell us there were a number of things that didn't fit. The street had been blocked off just before the incident. Once the crowd was let in and had lined up, the media appeared but kept their distance. The attack took place and the media were immediately on the scene. The majority of people killed are alleged to be 'tame' Serbs. Who knows? The only thing for sure is that innocent people were killed." [Interpretation] Is this, regardless of the more precise statements by General MacKenzie later on, is it clear that here what this is about is that it was a construed attack, because he says quite clearly: [In English] "The street had been blocked off just before the incident --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tendentious or leading or both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, I think you have to formulate your question differently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Every time you begin "is it clear..." it is almost certain that you're leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. I won't start my questions with "is it clear..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here, Mr. Barriot: "The streets had been blocked off just before the incident. [In English] Once the crowd was let in and had lined up, the media appeared but kept their distance. The attack took place and the media were immediately on the scene." [Interpretation] Then it says the tame Serbs were killed. What does that tell us, then, Mr. Barriot?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is not ambiguous. Lewis Mackenzie's story is clear the Serbs were not responsible for this explosion. This is what UNPROFOR people were saying at the time, and this is what has been corroborated by a number of Canadian military who were close to General MacKenzie. I would like to say, by the way, that Mrs. Carla Del Ponte only mentioned the 27th of May 1992 attack because the only person who challenged the responsibility of the Serbs was General MacKenzie, whereas Markale 1 and Markale 2 we have a series of statements by generals and officers who dispute the responsibility of the Serbs in these attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Barriot. Now, let's take a look at General Wahlgren's letter which Madam Del Ponte also presented to us. The letter is addressed to Goran Hadzic. We're not challenging that, are we? That's not in dispute. No, right. Then and page 2, that is to say at the end of the letter, the last paragraph says the following: "I'm also writing [In English] the other party to this conflict in respect of breaches emanating from their military activity." So that second page -- I'm sorry. The other side is the Croatian side. I assume that's not in dispute either.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this can be challenged in any way. This letter was written in 1993 after the attack against the Miljevaca plateau in 1992 and after the attacks that were launched in January 1993 against Ravni Kotari and Netica [phoen] and this entire region, and this continued throughout 1993. Hundred or so people died in the offensive and Ravni Kotari and Netica, so it's quite obvious when he writes on the 1st of April, 1993, what he has primarily in mind is the Croat attacks against the UN protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But -- well, that's part of the matter, but here we're talking about two parties, one we have the Republika Srpska Krajina, he addresses Goran Hadzic; and the other party is the Croatian party, the Croatian side. Is there Yugoslavia, Serbia, Belgrade, anything like that here? Any third side, third party, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing is mentioned about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It shows that the lieutenant intended to be even-handed in this matter. He was going to report crimes on both sides. Mr. Milosevic, we are pretty near to 2.00. We are about 15, 20 minutes beyond the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am bearing that in mind, but we have been presented with a few documents here, and the document that -- one of the documents by Lieutenant Colonel or Colonel - I can't remember the rank exactly now - Eremija -- can we see who it's addressed to, because -- do we see that? Because it mentions a JNA officer. The date is the 23rd of October, 1991. 23rd of October, therefore, 1991. That was the time when the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was still in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. At that time, in 1991, the only legitimate army was the JNA, the one of the Yugoslav Federation, which had less than 50 per cent of Serbs, comprised less than 50 per cent of Serbs. In the summer of 1991, I'd like to stress the fact that a number of attacks were launched and a number of the Slovenian and Croatian secessionists did massacre a number of JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we see from this that this JNA officer is addressing his higher command, that is to say the command of the military district of the JNA? Would that be right, of that legitimate army of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to say that a number of these officers were Croats, and let's say that some of them deserted the JNA to go and fight against their own army. In other words, they deserted before, they had deserted awhile before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like to draw your attention to something else. Lieutenant colonel, a lieutenant colonel of the JNA, assistant commander of a certain unit is writing to the commander of the 1st Army of the 1st Military District, as it was then, in the SFRY, and in item 5 he says proposals for improving morale in the units, and he goes on to speak of, in point 1 of that same paragraph 5, that they should undertake the organised disarming of paramilitary formations, and then goes on to enumerate them and proposes that the authorities of the Republic of Serbia must participate in the campaign. So as far as I can say -- see, the Republic of Serbia is only mentioned here within the context of the proposal of measures made by this commander that if it deals with Serb citizens who might be somewhere in that territory. Is there anywhere else in this document where we can deduce that this has anything at all to do with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And let's have a look at this report. As far as I can understand, it was General Nambiar's report. In paragraph 2, reference is made to the incursion of the Croatian army on the 21st of June, and in point 3, Sector West is referred to. "[In English]... armed elements from the Croatian side to cross the Sava River and attack Bosnian Serb elements south of the river." "... Croatian side across the Sava River and attack Bosnian Serb elements south of --" [Interpretation] So that was point 2. And then 3(a) and 3(b) it says attacked by the Croatian army, the 3rd of August, again Sector East. Then in the middle of (d): "[In English] Prisoners interviewed by UNPROFOR said that they had been mobilised and trained by the Croatian army in certain areas in Croatian and were being infiltrated in small groups into Bosnia and Herzegovina to join in the fighting there." [Interpretation] So this entire chapter, the first chapter, speaks of violations of cease-fire. All of this has to do with violations. I skipped over (c), subparagraph (c). That's the only one, and it says: "[In English] On 21 August 1992, three Serbs so-called 'border militia' personnel were shot dead in the vicinity of the confrontation line in Sector East." [Interpretation] So the entire chapter has to do with cease-fire violations. Can you find a single subparagraph where it shows that Serbs had violated the cease-fire? You have the entire chapter to deal with. It's -- the report starts with it. Is there a single reference to any Serb violations of the cease-fire? Try to find one.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't find any. And anyway, throughout my testimony I mentioned on various occasions all the cease-fire violations by the Croatian forces, especially in 1992, in 1993, against the UNPAs. So all these cease-fire violations in 1992, in 1993 were by the Croatian forces. I also stressed how many infiltrations there were by the Croatian regular and irregular forces towards Bosnia and especially towards Bosnia and Herzegovina and towards the eastern -- the western part of Bosnia, especially with a view to carrying out the Storm operation which was supposed to put two groups on the flanks of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to read something out to you, parts of Resolution 802, dated 1993, Security Council Resolution 803 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 802, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is whether it is identical to what your own knowledge has been. Resolution 802, dated 1993, says: "[In English] Deeply concerned by the information provided by the Secretary-General to the Security Council on 25 of January, 1993, on the rapid and violent deterioration of the situation in Croatia as a result of military attacks by Croatian armed forces on the areas under the protection of the United Nations Protection Forces (UNPROFOR), "Strongly condemning those attacks which have led to casualties and loss of life in UNPROFOR, as well as among the civilian population, "Deeply concerned also by the lack of cooperation in recent months by the Serb local authorities in the area under protection of UNPROFOR --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're a little confused at the moment. This is Resolution 802.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's D66.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're dealing with the exhibit with Council Resolution 743 and 762.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he has moved on now to 802, which is D66.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: D66, if that was dealt with in cross-examination, can be dealt with in re-examination but arguably not otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have to bring to your attention the question of time. It's now almost ten minutes after two. We were scheduled to stop at 1.45. There is another case here that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We cannot go beyond another five minutes. So if we can't conclude with this witness, he will have to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right then, I'm going to skip all of this, Medak investigation, the United Nations Security Council Annex 7 -- "[In English] 28th of December, 1994." [Interpretation] And then, "[In English] ... of the military operation of the Republic of Croatia." [Interpretation] And so on, and then about Medak in September 1993. I think -- let me just read --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, fundamentally is there a question being formulated at the moment? He's just reading things out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's the problem. That's the problem. You're reading from the Resolution. You're not formulating a question. I don't wish to rush you. I mean, if you're not through with your examination-in-chief, then the witness will have to return tomorrow morning, although I would imagine that would be quite regrettable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to finish with this question now. All right. Let's let the witness go. So I'm just going to read four more lines from this UN document. "[In English] ... September about 600 Croat forces attacked the pocket and artillery mortar and/or tank fire barrage preceded an infantry and tank advance. Croats attacked from the north-east and quickly killed or routed a few Serb defenders. Overrunning the Serb defences, the Croat forces soon captured Divoselo, Citluk, Donje Selo and surrounding villages. By 10th of September, Croatian army was in charge of the area."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this correspond to the knowledge you have about the attacks against the zones and this pocket of Medak in general? What do you know about this? All of these are UN documents, documents. Does this correspond to your own knowledge from the time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does correspond perfectly and it does corroborate my testimony. We back then in September 1993 in the Medak pocket. This is the third aggression by the Croatian forces again the UNPAs. This was the Scorched Earth operation, headed by General Bobetko, who himself admitted in the book that he wrote, All My Battles is the title, he admitted that the attack on the Medak pocket had been planned at the highest level within the Croatian state and many generals took part in the operation, among them Mirko Norac, Agim Ceku, and Ante Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Barriot. I'm going to skip of rest of my questions in order to be able to finish today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Barriot, for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence. Your testimony is concluded, and you may leave. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of January, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.13 p.m.,
